#9582. ‘Mariko Mori anticipated the zeitgeist’: curator Alexandra Munroe on her new show and how Japan's art scene has changed

Mariko Mori’s Birth of a Star (1995) Courtesy Mori Art Museum

The US curator Alexandra Munroe has three decades of experience working closely with Japanese institutions, going back to her landmark survey Japanese Art after 1945: Scream Against the Sky at the Yokohama Museum of Art in 1994. Now she is back in the country as the co-curator of the current Mariko Mori retrospective at the Mori Art Museum in Tokyo. The show is a collaboration with the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, where she is a senior curator at large, and has been co-curated with the Mori Art Museum’s director Mami Kataoka.

The Art Newspaper: How has Japan’s museum ecology changed over the years?

Alexandra Munroe: It’s changed enormously. The Yokohama Museum of Art opened in 1989, anticipating the museum boom of the 1990s when municipalities and prefectures across Japan were opening new institutions with extraordinary buildings designed by architects like Fumihiko Maki, Arata Isozaki and others.

Although there were important precursors like the Museum of Modern Art, Kamakura, established in 1951, and the National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo, established in 1952, there was remarkably little concerted historical understanding of Modern and contemporary Japanese art and its role in global art history. Around the early 1990s, curators and scholars were piecing together how such art had evolved under the umbrella of post-war society—defeat in the Second World War, reconstruction, Americanisation—as well as through the contributions of Japanese artists abroad like Yoko Ono, Yayoi Kusama and On Kawara. The new museums contributed to the tremendous growth of the field, both within Japan and internationally.

Curator Alexandra Munroe © Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, New York/David Heald

Successive institutions have built on that legacy. It’s been gratifying to see the Mori Art Museum develop into a global museum under the trailblazing leadership of Mami Kataoka. The recent Sou Fujimoto exhibition was one of the greatest architectural shows I’ve ever seen, while the solo shows of Louise Bourgeois, Ai Weiwei and Lee Bul, going back 20 years now, are among the most influential for those artists staged anywhere in the world.

All of this has been aided by the simultaneous transformation of the gallery scene, with a proliferation of experimental galleries since 1994, not to mention international galleries representing Japanese artists or movements like Gutai, Mono-ha and Neo-Pop. I also appreciate the role that Benesse Art Site Naoshima has played, through the vision of patron Soichiro Fukutake, in the emergence of Japan as a contemporary art superpower. Only a few hundred people attended the opening of Benesse House Museum in 1992. Now events like the Setouchi Triennale draw millions to the islands when the home population is a few thousand. And Benesse’s commissioning programme has given artists like Yukinori Yanagi, Rei Naito and Shinro Ohtake a platform for staging their most ambitious works.

Recent decades have seen a remarkable expansion of museums in China and Korea, Southeast Asia and the Gulf. At the same time, institutions around the world are facing new challenges with austerity measures and a withdrawal of public support for art. What lessons can Japan offer other art scenes?

I have great admiration—and some envy—for the public funding of Japanese art museums. The Japanese model of collecting regionally yet within an international context is something to emulate. There’s also something to be said for collections focusing on artists whose histories were shaped by the places where they grew up and, in some cases, ran away from. The Nagoya City Art Museum has extraordinary holdings of On Kawara’s works, including rare early reportage pieces, even though he left the region in his teens. The Ashiya City Museum of Art and History’s collection of Gutai is unparalleled in the world. And the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum, under the guidance of curators like Kuroda Raiji, has sought to map and reimagine artistic exchanges in Asia.I commend all the brilliant scholarship that has emerged out of these enterprises.

That said, in recent years Japan has retreated from its post-war identification as an international country. One motivation for doing the Mori show is to stimulate a revival in collaborations that can help bring the work done in Japan into international circulation.

Mariko Mori’s Play with Me (1994) Courtesy Mori Art Museum

Collaborations between Japanese and international institutions typically take the form of touring shows, whereas intensive co-productions are rare. How did the collaboration between the Guggenheim and the Mori Art Museum come about?

It’s called synergy! In the summer of 2024 both Mami Kataoka and I had begun talking to Mariko Mori about staging a retrospective and we combined forces. Mariko rose to meteoric stardom in the 1990s for Cyborg (1994-95), the first of her series of photomurals inserting herself as a cyborg, and later a Buddhist-inflected deity, into digitally rendered settings. That interest in technology subsequently found form in complex multisensory environments like Wave UFO (1999-2002), the first artwork to incorporate brainwave biofeedback.

I was interested in reappraising Mariko’s work in the current context of technology-based art, specifically digital technologies. Technology is not an obstacle to humanism for her, but a means of envisioning a new kind of humanism that allows for higher states of consciousness. At the same time, Mariko’s engagement with [pre-historic Japanese] Jōmon culture, alternative belief systems and the afterlife resonates with Indigenous and First Nations artists incorporating Indigenous knowledge into critiques of Western epistemes of modernity and linear time.

For her part, Mami has a longstanding interest in art that addresses spirituality in the modern era, which opens up a critique of the dominant trends of contemporary art as established by market forces and Western institutions, so I think Mariko’s work felt urgent to that curatorial research and practice.

Yes. Collaboration is integral to Guggenheim programmes like the Asian Art Initiative and the UBS MAP Global Art Initiative. We have consistently partnered with museums, curators and artists across Asia to help us collectively think through the larger argument of global art history and how to present exhibitions that map histories and ideas beyond the Eurocentric canon. The collaboration with the Mori is a direct outcome of that, and I’d say it’s a direct outcome of the Mori’s profoundly international outlook as well.

Alexandra Munroe with Japanese artist Yoko Ono at the AICA (International Association of Art Critics) Awards ceremony, New York, in 2001 Courtesy Alexandra Munroe

A compelling retrospective does not just look back but also shows how the artist was ahead of their time. In what ways have we finally caught up with Mariko Mori?

Mariko’s work resonates with the writings of the contemporary philosopher Yuk Hui, who argues for a holistic understanding of technology grounded in Eastern thought and cosmologies, or “cosmotechnics”, as opposed to its bifurcation in modern Western traditions. Mariko anticipated that zeitgeist as a Japanese woman artist who conducted deep research into schools of thought like Pure Land Buddhism and Jōmon cosmology alongside contemporary sciences of the mind.

These are areas of enormous interest to artists now. Look at LuYang, a young Chinese artist who is a serious practitioner of Tantric Buddhism and uses game engines to illustrate themes of transmigration of the soul, multiple selves and the world as an illusion. The Korean new media artist Ayoung Kim also looks up to Mariko for unabashedly drawing parallels between art and technology as ways to “recalibrate our reality”, as Ayoung told me.

I think there will be an enthusiastic response to Mariko’s work from younger artists who are interested in storytelling and altered states of mind, artists who are seeking to break free of the lingering hang-ups of Western art, and anyone looking to just get away to another world.

#9581. Increased Risk for Suicide Attempts Among Children Who Use Tobacco Products

Children who report the use of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes and vaping — have a 3 to 5 times increased risk for suicide attempts (SAs), according to study results published in JAMA Network Open.

New tobacco products (ie, e-cigarettes, vapes, hookahs) have become increasingly popular in the United States, particularly among children and adolescents. Although it is well-documented that adolescents and adults who smoke cigarettes have an increased likelihood of suicidality, it is unclear whether this heightened risk applies to children who use tobacco products.

To address this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a cross-sectional cohort study from September 1 to September 5, 2022. The researchers used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a nationally representative cohort of 11,868 US children enrolled at 9 and 10 years of age. The objective of the current study was to investigate the correlation between tobacco product use and the incidence of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation (SI), and SAs among preadolescent children. Substance use was evaluated using the ABCD Youth Substance Use Interview and hair toxicology tests at baseline, a 6-month follow-up, and then yearly. The researchers assessed suicidality using children and caregiver reports of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS-5).

The researchers included data from 8988 children (median age, 9.8 years; 47.9% girls). At baseline, 1.1% of children reported ever using tobacco products, and this prevalence rose significantly to 1.7% at the 18-month follow-up. The researchers observed no statistical difference in smoking experience by sex or race/ethnicity; however, tobacco-using children generally came from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, had greater prenatal smoking exposure, and were more likely to have parents with a history of depression, alcohol issues, and behavioral or suicide-related problems, relative to children who did not use tobacco products.

The researchers observed significant associations between tobacco product use among children and increased risks for SAs at each time point. Tobacco use was linked to a 3 to 5 times higher risk for SAs, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.67 (95% CI, 2.35-9.27; P <.001) at baseline, 4.25 (95% CI, 2.33-7.74; P <.001) at 1 year, and 2.85 (95% CI, 1.58-5.12; P =.001) at year 2.

The researchers also evaluated whether children’s personality, cognition, and psychological outcomes were associated with tobacco product use. They found that children were more likely to endorse tobacco use if they had conduct disorder (P <.001), oppositional defiant disorder (P <.001), rule-breaking behaviors (P <.001), aggressive behaviors (P <.001), social problems (P =.009), attention problems (P =.02), as well as personality traits of lack of planning (P <.001), positive urgency (P =.006), lack of perseverance (P =.009), sensation seeking (P =.02), aggression (P =.02), negative urgency (P =.03), and depressive mood (P <.05).

However, the association between tobacco use and SAs remained elevated, independent of these behavioral/psychopathology traits (OR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.70-5.65; P <.001) in regression analyses. Conversely, the association between tobacco use and SI was not sustained when childhood behavioral measures were considered.

Among other substance use, only alcohol sipping was independently associated with SAs (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.13; P =.007). These findings suggest that while other substance use is related to SAs, tobacco product use remains a robust independent risk factor.

Study authors concluded, “The findings suggest that smoking tobacco products may be a modifiable risk factor that can be addressed in suicide prevention efforts, especially among children.”

These study findings may be limited by the use of hair toxicology tests to assess tobacco use and the inability to determine causality, given the observational study design.

Lee PH, Tervo-Clemmens B, Liu RT, et al. Use of tobacco products and suicide attempts among elementary school-aged children. JAMA Netw Open. Published online February 5, 2024. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.0376

#9580. The Urgency of Early ADHD Intervention

Delaying treatment for ADHD until the teen years comes with potential life-long consequences. Here’s what you should know.

Q: I believe my elementary school-age child has ADHD, but my husband doesn’t think so. He refuses to get our child evaluated. I have ADHD and I know this can run in families. What should I do?

This question reflects a dilemma faced by many families: What happens when one parent wants possible signs of ADHD evaluated while another prefers to wait and see? The answer may matter more than many people realize.

Imagine two children entering first grade:

Jacob is bright, curious, and energetic. He struggles to sit still, frequently forgets to turn in his homework, and has difficulty following multi-step instructions. His teacher notices the symptoms and relays these to his parents. Jacob’s pediatrician conducts a comprehensive evaluation and diagnoses Jacob with ADHD.

His parents learn strategies to support him at home. His school implements accommodations. Later, medication becomes part of his treatment plan. Jacob still faces challenges, but he learns how his brain works and develops tools to succeed. He graduates from high school with strong grades and heads off to college.

[Webinar Replay: “6 Principles for Raising a Child with ADHD”]

Now imagine Maya. She is also intelligent, but her suspected ADHD symptoms present differently. She daydreams in class and quietly falls behind. She is emotionally sensitive, often taking criticism to heart and becoming overwhelmed by setbacks that her peers seem to brush off. Her teachers describe her as capable but inconsistent. Because she isn’t disruptive, her struggles are attributed to a lack of effort, disorganization, anxiety, or immaturity.

Year after year, she works harder while feeling increasingly frustrated. As academic demands increase, so do her feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy. By the time she receives an ADHD diagnosis at age 16, her grades have suffered, her confidence has eroded, and she is considering leaving school altogether.

The paths of these two children, one who received early intervention with medication and one who remained untreated until her mid-teens, illustrate a growing concern in ADHD care: It’s not simply about whether children are diagnosed, but when.

[Self-Test: Could Your Preschooler Have ADHD?]

A recent study published in JAMA Psychiatry examined educational outcomes among more than 580,000 individuals with ADHD. The researchers found that children diagnosed earlier in life had significantly better educational outcomes than those diagnosed during adolescence. Earlier diagnosis with associated with higher grade point averages, a greater likelihood of pursuing academic educational tracks, and substantially lower rates of school dropout.

The differences were striking. Individuals diagnosed during the early elementary school years had school dropout rates of approximately 9 percent by age 20, compared with nearly 30 percent among those first diagnosed around age 16. Similar patterns were observed in both males and females. The researchers concluded that adolescents diagnosed later represent a particularly vulnerable group.

The findings do not suggest that a diagnosis alone changes a child’s future. Rather, earlier recognition creates opportunities for intervention. Children identified sooner can access school accommodations, behavioral supports, parent education, and, when appropriate, medication – before years of academic struggles, self-doubt, and declining confidence take hold and begin to shape their identity.

This raises an important question: How many Mayas are sitting in classrooms today, struggling silently while waiting years for recognition or a diagnosis?

Universal ADHD screening offers a potential solution. Many children with ADHD are identified only after academic, social, or emotional difficulties have become impossible to ignore. Screening creates an opportunity to recognize concerns earlier before the consequences of undiagnosed ADHD begin to accumulate. Importantly, screening is not diagnosis. It is simply an invitation to look more closely.

Many critics of universal screening worry about overdiagnosis or unnecessary labeling. Those concerns deserve consideration. However, screening itself does not determine whether a child has ADHD. It merely identifies children who may benefit from a more comprehensive evaluation, meaning that fewer children with significant challenges get overlooked.

Growing evidence suggests that every year of delayed recognition carries educational and emotional costs that are difficult to reverse. Universal screening will not identify every child. But it may help more children find the right path before they wander too far afield.

For many children, the greatest risk may not be receiving an ADHD diagnosis. It may be never receiving one at all.

Greg Mattingly, M.D., is an associate clinical professor at Washington University School of Medicine and co-chair of U.S. Psych Congress.

#9577. Life mirrors art: the story of Yayoi Kusama

Kusama in the first of her signature Infinity Room pieces, Infinity Mirror Room—Phalli’s Field (1965) at Castellane Gallery, New York © Yayoi Kusama

When Yayoi Kusama died in Tokyo on 14 August, aged 97, she left behind a legacy almost unparalleled in contemporary art. The Japanese artist, who arrived in New York in 1958 as an outsider—female, Asian and largely unknown—eventually became one of the most recognisable artists on the planet. Her dots and pumpkins migrated from canvases and sculptures onto handbags and shopfronts; her Infinity Mirror Rooms generated queues around museums and millions of selfies.

Yet Kusama’s visibility has, when it comes to the structures that once excluded her, remained extraordinary.

“Kusama’s global success has had enormous symbolic force,” says Izumi Nakajima, an art historian specialising in feminism and post-war Japanese art. “Yet the exceptional success of an individual woman artist and a structural transformation in the gendered and geographical asymmetries of the art world operate on different registers.” A canon, Nakajima adds, can accommodate “a small number of monumental women artists while continuing to marginalise a far larger number of women”.

That distinction complicates the familiar story of Kusama as a trailblazer for women and Asian artists. Japan in the 1950s and early 60s, Nakajima says, had a substantial cohort of women pursuing experimental practices, including Atsuko Tanaka and Hideko Fukushima. To project Kusama’s present fame backwards risks producing a history in which she appears uniquely radical from the outset. Kusama’s departure from Japan in 1957 was crucial: while Japan’s high-growth era increasingly reorganised women’s lives around domesticity, she pursued her career abroad, relentlessly making both her art and herself visible through exhibitions, photographs, fashion, happenings and the media.

For the Tokyo- and Vienna-based feminist and queer publishing and research collective Multiple Spirits, the transformation since Kusama’s early career is nevertheless real. Compared with a global art world then dominated overwhelmingly by white men, opportunities to encounter artists from different backgrounds have unquestionably expanded, the collective says. But it questions whether Kusama’s trajectory should still function as a model of “success” when the criteria by which success is measured remain largely inherited from that same art world. “Values and measures different from those shaped by a white male-centred art world are still insufficient,” the collective says.

Nor does Nakajima see Kusama fitting comfortably into another role frequently assigned to her: that of the feminist icon. Rather than treating feminism as “an attribute or categorical designation”, Nakajima argues, it is more productive to use it as a critical method through which to read her work. Kusama’s repetition, sexuality, self-representation and negotiation of the body all invite feminist interpretation. But unlike strands of feminist art that rejected Modernism’s claims to autonomy and universality, Kusama repeatedly resisted being circumscribed as either a “woman” or a “Japanese” artist. “She sought to occupy the position of the universal artistic subject that Modernism had imagined,” Nakajima says.

The Multiple Spirits collective similarly notes a gap between Kusama’s international reception and her popular image at home. In Japan, it says, she is less commonly understood as a feminist icon than as the creator of colourful polka-dotted paintings and installations. The politics of her 1960s happenings—their anti-war messages and calls for sexual liberation—have received comparatively less attention. Rather than reducing Kusama to an individual “feminist” or “queer” identity, the collective argues that these radical practices need to be reconsidered within the social and cultural conditions that produced them.

Another paradox lies in Kusama’s transformation from avant-garde provocateur to global cultural brand. In 1966, she appeared uninvited at the Venice Biennale with Narcissus Garden, offering mirrored spheres for sale beneath a sign declaring “Your Narcissism for Sale”. Decades later, the mirrors themselves became among contemporary art’s most coveted attractions. Visitors queue for hours to spend seconds inside an Infinity Mirror Room, phone in hand, while collaborations with Louis Vuitton turned her dots into a globally recognisable luxury motif. Critics have consequently cast Kusama as both a precursor of the immersive “artainment” economy and one of its most successful brands.

For Hidenori Ota, the founder of the gallery Ota Fine Arts and Kusama’s longtime representative in Japan, the artist’s embrace of visibility cannot be separated from the struggle to make herself heard. “I imagine that, in order to deliver a voice that otherwise could not reach people, she first needed to make her own presence larger,” he says. Having directly experienced war, Ota suggests, Kusama sought a language capable of reaching a mass audience, repeatedly returning to the word “love” as a vehicle for criticism.

Kusama and a life-size replica, from her collaboration with Louis Vuitton © Yayoi Kusama

Kusama’s popularity also made mental illness unusually visible within mainstream contemporary art. She voluntarily lived at a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo from 1977 onward, working for decades at a nearby studio. While frequently connecting her compulsive repetition and artistic production to hallucinations and psychological distress, she generally eschewed disability advocacy. Narratives around Kusama have drawn criticism for reproducing the familiar trope of the “mad genius” who triumphs over adversity, while doing relatively little to address disability, psychiatric experience or accessibility. Nakajima similarly warns against narratives that link women’s creativity to illness, trauma and psychological compulsion: such frameworks, she says, have historically helped women artists gain recognition while simultaneously restricting how their practices are understood.

Perhaps the most troubling asterisk in Kusama’s legacy relates to her descriptions of Black people in her 2002 autobiography, Infinity Net. In the original Japanese edition, she blamed Black residents and unhoused people for the decline of her New York neighbourhood. That, along with other denigrating lines, was omitted from the 2011 English translation. When the comments received renewed attention ahead of her 2023 exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Kusama said she “deeply regret[ted] using hurtful and offensive language” and apologised for the pain she had caused.

The episode sits uneasily beside the universalist language of love that characterised Kusama’s later public persona. Asked how it should shape her legacy, Ota says: “Rather than simply viewing her through that label of ‘racist’, [her words] should be examined in relation to the social conditions and historical context of the time.” He adds that it requires further debate and study. The controversy nevertheless underscores the limits of transforming a complex historical figure into an uncomplicated symbol of inclusion.

Ota is likewise sceptical of attributing subsequent changes in Asia’s art world to a single artist. “Rather than Kusama changing things herself, I think the larger shifts of the era—particularly the social and economic rise of Asia—were more significant,” he says. “She moved in step with those larger changes.”

Kusama’s 1967 “happening”, Body Festival, in which polka dot-painted participants danced in public New York spaces © Yayoi Kusama

The Multiple Spirits collective flags how, in Japan and beyond, as shrinking cultural budgets require museums to pursue larger audiences and alternative funding sources, Kusama shows became reliable for producing economic results. But her visibility has not particularly helped other marginalised artists. “We cannot entrust structural change in the art world to the success story of a minority artist,” the collective says. What matters instead are less spectacular changes: improving working conditions and accessibility, using inclusive language, protecting freedom of expression and connecting such efforts across institutions.

Kusama entered a Western, male-dominated art world and ultimately became bigger than almost any artist within it. But “exceptional success and structural inequality can coexist”, Nakajima observes. Kusama changed who could occupy the centre of contemporary art, but not the nature of that centre.

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, physicians continue to experience burnout at alarmingly high rates. In a recent survey of 2440 physicians, approximately 63% of respondents reported having at least 1 manifestation of burnout in 2021; this was higher than all 4 prior assessment time points since 2011.1 Because physician burnout is more common in certain specialties, it is crucial to identify trends and offer help to those at higher risk. This article examines the symptoms, causes, and prevalence of burnout among clinicians in various specialties, and outlines strategies physicians can use to address burnout.

For many clinicians, symptoms of burnout were accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, chronic stress due to work overload, exposure to infected patients, lack of protective equipment, and poor efforts to control infection rates increased the risk of burnout.3 Other factors associated with burnout include system inefficiencies, administrative burdens, and increased regulation and technology requirements.2

The consequences of physician burnout affect patients as well as clinicians. From a patient’s perspective, physician burnout can result in poor physician/patient rapport, adherence to treatment, and treatment outcomes.4 For physicians, burnout can lead to declining mental health and subsequent depression, substance abuse, and suicide.4

Although burnout affects clinicians in all specialties and practice settings, the rate is higher in certain specialties. The AMA’s Organization Biopsy® is an assessment tool large health care organizations can use to measure and improve the health of their organizations.5 One of the parameters this tool measures is burnout.

Medscape conducts an annual survey on physician lifestyle and happiness that includes questions about burnout and depression. Burnout was reported by a higher proportion of women (51%) than men (38%). The 3 largest factors contributing to burnout among emergency medicine physicians were having too many bureaucratic tasks (51%), a lack of respect from patients (50%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (46%).8

Slightly more than one-half of female family physicians (51%) and one-third of male family physicians (33%) reported experiencing burnout.9 The overall proportion of respondents who said they felt burned out was 42%. Depression affected 4% of family medicine physicians, while 15% said they felt both burned out and depressed.9

By far the largest contributor to family physician burnout was having too many bureaucratic tasks; 73% of respondents reported tasks such as paperwork and charting were the main culprit. Working too many hours and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff were cited as factors contributing to burnout by 36% and 31% of respondents, respectively.9

Overall, 39% of pediatricians reported feeling burned out.11 More female pediatricians reported feeling burned out more than their male counterparts (46% vs 26%, respectively).10 The proportion of respondents who said they felt depressed was 3%, while 19% reported being both burned out and depressed.

The 3 largest contributors to burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (65%), lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (40%), and spending too many hours at work (38%).10

In Medscape’s 2023 report, obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported the following11:

Obstetrics and gynecology physicians reported that the 3 largest contributors to their burnout were having too many bureaucratic tasks (56%), spending too many hours at work (47%), and a lack of respect from administrators/employers, colleagues, or staff (42%).11

#9575. What Narcissists, Psychopaths And Sadists Have In Common

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Different dark personalities may have more in common than their labels suggest.

Narcissists, psychopaths, sadists and manipulative people share a dark personality core that predicts selfish and antisocial choices.

This common tendency helps explain whether people exploit others, retaliate against them or refuse to trust them.

The crucial feature is a willingness to pursue personal interests at other people’s expense, accompanied by beliefs that justify doing so.

Known as the dark factor of personality, or D, this tendency brings together traits that can look quite different on the surface.

Narcissism involves an inflated sense of self-importance, Machiavellianism centres on manipulation, psychopathy includes callousness, and sadism involves enjoying others’ suffering.

The idea that these traits share an underlying disposition was established in earlier research examining their overlap and links to harmful behaviour (Moshagen et al., 2018).

The latest findings suggest that this shared core is more consistently associated with antisocial decisions than any of the four traits considered separately.

In other words, knowing what these personalities have in common may reveal more about their choices than knowing which particular label fits them.

The research involved over 10,000 people across ten studies using eight types of decision-making game.

Participants completed personality questionnaires before making hypothetical choices involving another person they did not know.

Depending on the game, they could decide how much money to share, whether to return someone’s trust, whether to retaliate or whether to cooperate.

Some situations allowed people to benefit themselves at someone else’s expense, while others explored whether they would trust another person when cooperation could benefit both.

People scoring higher on the dark factor consistently made fewer prosocial choices across all eight games.

The individual dark traits also generally predicted less prosocial behaviour, but their associations were weaker.

Once their shared dark core was taken into account, the separate traits usually added little to the explanation.

There were a few exceptions, particularly involving Machiavellianism in situations where distrust could influence decisions.

One possible explanation is that dark personality traits combine harmful tendencies with other characteristics that are not inherently antisocial.

For example, boldness does not necessarily involve harming anyone, while wanting admiration does not automatically mean exploiting others.

Earlier research proposed that these additional characteristics help distinguish dark traits from one another, while their shared core captures what makes them socially harmful (Bader et al., 2023).

Measuring a broad trait such as psychopathy may therefore mix callous self-interest with features that have little relevance to a particular moral decision.

Focusing on the common core could provide a clearer picture of someone’s willingness to disregard other people’s welfare.

Importantly, the dark factor extends beyond wanting a larger share of the rewards.

It also encompasses a readiness to hurt others and beliefs that can make selfish conduct seem acceptable.

Distrust may fit this pattern because expecting other people to behave selfishly can provide a convenient justification for doing the same.

That is a proposed psychological explanation, rather than evidence that distrust caused the choices observed here.

The findings do not mean that everyone with dark traits will behave selfishly in every situation.

Nor do they establish that personality caused the decisions participants made.

All the games were hypothetical, so participants were describing what they would choose rather than making decisions with real financial consequences.

This matters because associations between dark traits and antisocial choices can be stronger in hypothetical situations than when money is genuinely at stake.

Participants also volunteered through a website offering dark-personality assessments, so they were not a representative sample of the wider population.

Even with these qualifications, the results support a simpler account of apparently different dark personalities: much of their connection to harmful choices lies in the same underlying disregard for others.

The study was published in the journal Judgment and Decision Making (Hilbig & Thielmann, 2025).

#9573. Documenta 16 hires four new curators

Left to right: Osei Bonsu, Raven Chacon, Noam Segal and Timea Junghaus

Bonsu: © Gas Foundation; Chacon: © Neal Santos; Segal: © Samantha Casolari; Junghaus: © Zoltan Adam

The curatorial team for Documenta 16 is expanding with the announcement of four new appointments. The new team members are the composer and installation artist Raven Chacon, who was named curator-at-large, alongside the curators and art historians Osei Bonsu, Timea Junghaus and Noam Segal, who were appointed curatorial advisers.

The next edition of the influential quinquennial contemporary art exhibition, which will take place next year (12 June-19 September) in Kassel, is led by Naomi Beckwith, the deputy director and chief curator of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.

Her team of four women curators—Carla Acevedo-Yates, Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, and Xiaoyu Weng—will develop the exhibition, publications and programming for the upcoming edition.

The artistic team for documenta 16: Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, Xiaoyu Weng, Carla Acevedo-Yates, and Naomi Beckwith

© documenta and Museum Fridericianum gGmbH / Photo: Nicolas Wefers

Chacon unveiled the two-mile-long land art installation Repellent Fence at the US/Mexico border in 2015; in 2022, he became the first Indigenous artist to be awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Bonsu is senior curator of international art, Africa, and diaspora at Tate Modern, where he co-curated Nigerian Modernism in 2025.

Junghaus was the founding director of Gallery8 – Roma Contemporary Art Space in Budapest (2013–2017) and launched the European Roma Institute for Arts and Culture in Berlin in 2017. Segal serves as the LG Electronics associate curator at the Guggenheim Museum in New York and was previously the director of curatorial research in the Master’s programme for curatorial practice at the School of Visual Arts, New York.

According to an online statement, “the [Documenta 16] exhibition and programmes will honour artists as they navigate a world in turmoil, developing strategies and new possibilities for living together amid planetary indeterminacy. Improvisation, experimentation, and collective learning will open new paths.”

The last edition of Documenta in 2022 sparked controversy after two antisemitic images were found in the work People’s Justice (2000), by the Indonesian artist collective, Taring Padi. The work was removed from show and, in the following days, Documenta posted a statement that was attributed to the Jakarta-based collective ruangrupa, who curated the exhibition. It read in part: “We acknowledge that this was our error.”

#9572. The Everyday Nutrient Linked To 32% Lower Dementia Risk

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Your brain uses this nutrient for memory, but its relationship with dementia risk is more complicated than “more is better”.

Moderate intake of choline, a nutrient found in eggs, fish and legumes, is linked to a lower risk of dementia.

Older adults consuming moderately high amounts had a 32 percent lower dementia risk than those consuming the least.

However, the highest intake was not associated with a clear benefit, suggesting that more is not necessarily better.

The research followed over 5,000 American adults, whose average age was almost 69, for around eight years.

Participants were initially free of dementia but around 500 developed the condition during follow-up.

After dividing participants into five groups according to choline intake, the researchers found a 32 percent lower dementia risk in the second-highest group than in the lowest, after accounting for other factors.

However, there was no statistically clear reduction in the highest-intake group.

The result therefore points towards a potentially beneficial range, rather than a steady fall in risk with every increase in consumption.

The researchers then combined their results with four previous studies to assess the broader pattern.

Together, these followed almost 138,000 people and recorded around 2,500 cases of dementia.

In the combined analysis, dementia risk fell as choline intake rose to approximately 465 milligrams per day, with no further reduction beyond that level.

Choline helps the brain produce acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory.

It also supplies building blocks for the membranes surrounding brain cells, helping maintain their structure and communication.

These roles could help explain a link between choline and cognitive ageing, although they do not prove that consuming more prevents dementia.

The nutrient also participates in processes that regulate homocysteine, a substance linked to problems with blood vessels and cognitive function.

Eggs, meat, poultry and nuts were among the main sources of choline in the American participants’ diets.

People consuming more choline obtained a greater proportion of it from eggs.

Crucially, the analysis assessed choline from food and did not include intake from supplements.

The findings therefore cannot establish whether choline supplements would lower dementia risk.

The study was published in the Nutrition Journal (Chen et al., 2026).

#9570. What’s Fogging Your Brain? Signs of Aging vs. ADHD

Cognitive changes may stem from perimenopause, ADHD, or early dementia, each of which requires distinct treatment.

Q: How do I know whether hormonal changes related to perimenopause are causing my cognitive function problems, or my ADHD is getting worse, or I might be experiencing mild cognitive impairment or early dementia?

ADHD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit clinically different cognitive deficits that help me differentiate one from the other. While ADHD symptoms involve forgetfulness, inattention, and distractibility, MCI has specific cognitive symptoms of word-finding challenges, misspellings, and the use of generic terms like “stuff” and “things” because of word-finding difficulty. Also, MCI is progressive over two to three years, whereas ADHD doesn’t generally worsen.

In perimenopause, a decline in estrogen leads to cognitive difficulties. In contrast to MCI, we know that the cognitive changes from estrogen decline are not the result of neurodegeneration.

However, the specific deficits related to declining estrogen haven’t been well differentiated from those associated with ADHD. So if you have pre-existing ADHD and you experience heightened cognitive difficulties in perimenopause and menopause, you may think, “My ADHD is getting worse.” But it’s likely not worsening ADHD. It’s declining estrogen.

Okay, so what do you do about it? There is a paucity of research for clinical guidance. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was not always recommended because it was alleged to increase risk for breast cancer and other illnesses. That claim has now been refuted by the most recent research, which has led to the removal of the black box warning from the FDA on HRT product labels. And so, if I have a female patient with ADHD who is 50 years old and says, “For the past two years, I’ve had cognitive decline,” the question to consider is this: “Do I increase her stimulant medication or do I put her on HRT?”

I am inclined at that point to put her on HRT for three months, keep her stimulant medication dosage stable, and monitor the qualitative changes in her cognitive functioning. If there is improvement on HRT, then the question becomes, “Does she stay on HRT for some extended period of time along with the stimulant medication?” If the HRT doesn’t work or she can’t take HRT for medical reasons, then I might increase the stimulant medication dosage to see if we can’t overcome the perimenopausal changes from the estrogen decline. This advice comes from my clinical experience, and it is unfortunate that we don’t have more research for clinical guidance here.

[Take This Self-Test: Is It Perimenopause or ADHD?]

Q: Could ADHD stimulant medication mask symptoms of mild cognitive impairment?

There is very limited research on stimulants and mild cognitive impairment (MCI). My clinical impression is that stimulants likely improve symptoms of MCI, but do not take that as an endorsement to seek treatment for MCI with stimulants. There is emerging research on MCI and stimulants that has not yet been published. The follow-up question to that is, if you have ADHD and MCI, will treating the ADHD delay the development of MCI or Alzheimer’s? There is no clinical research for me to answer that question. But if this were me, I’d be treating my ADHD, keeping my fingers crossed, and appreciating the fact that the quality of my life on medicine is better than it would be without my ADHD treated.

ADHD should not get worse; however, the experience of ADHD may be worse if life’s demands start to increase and exceed your ability to compensate. However, if you’re having cognitive changes that are beyond the scope of your ADHD, you may have two neurologic processes going on: your ADHD and something else. In this case, your ADHD may, indeed, be getting worse because you have a second neurological process that needs to be evaluated.

David W. Goodman, M.D., is an internationally recognized expert on adult ADHD.

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

The old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

What does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

The right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:

Fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

For those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

#9567. Collectors Cristina Chacón and Diego Uribe to open contemporary art space in Miami

The new DC Lab, Miami Courtesy DC Art Foundation

The Colombian collectors and philanthropists Cristina Chacón and Diego Uribe will open DC Lab, a new contemporary art space on Miami’s Bird Road, expanding their nonprofit DC Art Foundation.

The admission-free, 9,000-sq.-ft space will host projects by international galleries that do not have a permanent presence in Miami, alongside research and public programming. Opening just in time for Miami Art Week on 29 November, DC Lab will present the first major survey in Miami of the Cuban artist Carlos Garaicoa, the foundation’s current artist in residence.

Based in Miami, Bogotá and Madrid, longtime partners Chacón and Uribe view collecting as a means of supporting the art community. “For us, collecting has always been more than acquiring works and has focused on a commitment to contributing to the cultural ecosystem,” Uribe tells The Art Newspaper.

The couple’s collection includes more than 500 Modern and contemporary works from around the globe, and they support institutions in Miami and beyond. At the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, they sit on the chairman’s council and the American and Latin American acquisitions boards. They also serve on the Museo Reina Sofía’s international patronage board and on the boards of Bogotá’s Museo de Arte Moderno and Miami’s Coral Gables Museum.

In 2021, the couple founded the DC Art Foundation to support artists and connect Miami’s art scene with the international community beyond Miami Art Week. Since 2022, the foundation has run a residency programme for mid-career and established artists.

“The foundation was a vehicle for the residency programme we fund at a private residence,” Uribe says. “The intention is to bring to Miami artists that activate the community, promoting local and international exchange.” Past residents include the Spanish textile artist Sonia Navarro and the Colombian artist Miler Lagos.

Carlos Garaicoa Photo: Oak Taylor Smith, courtesy DC Art Foundation

DC Lab will include exhibition and education spaces as well as a library. “This is a laboratory where experimental ideas and projects can happen in the city,” Uribe says. “We created a novel residency model that provides international galleries with space to present mid-career and established artists new to Miami, potentially inspiring them to settle here.”

Chacón adds that while international galleries often participate in Art Basel Miami Beach and its various satellite fairs, DC Lab will enable more in-depth projects. It will also strengthen the foundation’s community-centred work. “In our residency programme, artists commit to an educational activity, and we often organise talks,” she says. “But this new venue allows for deeper community engagement.”

The opening exhibition at DC Lab, co-presented with Italy’s Galleria Continua and Mor Charpentier (based in Paris and Bogotá), links the new venue to the residency. “While the residency programme runs independently from DC Lab, Garaicoa’s residency was especially fitting for the opening,” Chacón says.

Garaicoa—known for addressing cultural and political issues through architecture, urbanism and history—will present works from his November residency as well as other recent projects. “My residency work relates to Miami, its architecture and growth,” he says, “reflecting how politics and language coexist in architecture.”

Passion is the key driver for Chacón and Uribe’s new space. “We are not trying to be a museum,” Uribe says. “We continue being a private foundation supporting the local community.”

Chacón adds: “For us, art is an incurable disease that lifts the soul.”

#9566. Q: “My Spouse Complains About My ADHD Constantly!”

“Start with an honest conversation that acknowledges the effects of your ADHD on your partner and explains how it thwarts your efforts to be the best possible spouse .”

Q: “How can I help my husband understand my ADHD so he’s not just complaining all the time about how hard this is for him?”

First, begin by acknowledging the truth of what he is saying: Your ADHD does, indeed, have tangible effects on him. It also has emotional effects; he likely burns much more mental energy than you can see worrying about whether you completed agreed-upon tasks.

Let down your guard for an honest conversation about the impact of your actions (or inaction) on him. Show him that he matters to you and that you empathize with his experience. You may need to spend significant time here; don’t move on until you’re positive that he really feels that you get it.

[Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship]

This sets the stage for the second part of the conversation — how ADHD thwarts your efforts to be the best possible partner. In other words, you have good intentions, even if they aren’t obvious, and you can feel equally frustrated and disappointed by what makes him upset. Also, your ADHD makes your life harder, not just his. While his complaints might be accurate, his too-frequent criticisms are not helping.

Finally, discuss how you can work together to address your hotspots. Ask: What can each of us do, or at least try to do, differently to smooth out some of our pain points? For example, do you want reminders? If so, how and when? Also, does he want to give those reminders?

It’s also helpful to discuss protocols when things don’t go according to plan. How and when can he bring up his concerns in a way that you can hear without getting defensive? How can you tell him that his proposed solution is not working for you?

Encourage your partner to focus on their experience rather than dissecting your actions and making declarations about why you did something.

For example, it’s more effective to say, “It stresses me out when you don’t follow through on commitments because then I feel like I have to take over, and I really don’t want to keep doing that,” versus saying, “You don’t worry about doing things because you know I’ll just do it if you don’t.”

[Download: 5 Ways to Improve Emotional Control at Home]

I often recommend focusing your conversations on what you want in the future, not what happened in the past.

#9565. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

#9564. New research reveals original colours of Ancient Egyptian shrine at Oxford museum

A digital projection will recolour the Shrine of Taharqa © Fisher Studios, 2026; courtesy Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford

A shrine built almost 3,000 years ago in northern Sudan will regain its original glowing colour later this month. Housed at the Ashmolean museum in Oxford, and the only freestanding building in Britain dating back to the time of the pharaohs, the Shrine of King Taharqa (690BC-654BC) will be recoloured through a digital projection that has been made after extensive research on surviving scraps and traces of pigment.

Fragments of red paint survive in crevices of the sandstone carvings, but microscopic analysis and hyperspectral imaging—combining photography and spectroscopy—also revealed evidence of colours now invisible to the naked eye, including yellow and “Egyptian blue”, a brilliant pigment used to depict divine figures.

According to Liam McNamara, the Ashmolean's keeper of antiquities, the carvings and inscriptions tell the story of the construction of the shrine: how the young Taharqa, later the king of Kush in Nubia and Pharaoh of Egypt, saw the ruins of the earlier brick temple to Amun-Re, built by Tutankhamen, with “the sand drifted to its roof”, as he journeyed north towards Thebes. At Taharqa's coronation he vowed to restore it and went on to build the shining new shrine within a new temple. Scorch marks on the stones of the shrine, also revealed in the project, bear witness to its eventual destruction in turn.

The Shrine of King Taharqa Courtesy of Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford

The relief carved sandstone blocks were originally plastered and brightly painted, showing Taharqa with the gods of Memphis, Heliopolis and also Amun-Re represented as both a Theban and a local Gematen deity. Taharqa himself is depicted both as an Egyptian pharaoh wearing the Double Crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, and in other scenes as a Kushite king with a ram’s head and sun disc earrings and the Kushite crown surmounted by two cobras.

The Shrine of King Taharqa came to Oxford from Khartoum in 150 crates 90 years ago as a gift from the Sudanese government to the Oxford University Excavations in Nubia, which had excavated it and other monuments over several seasons. It was given to the museum in 1936 by Nora Griffith, in memory of her husband Francis Llewellyn Griffith, who had led—and largely paid for—the expeditions. He had taught himself Ancient Egyptian at Oxford since there was no department, and went on to become the first professor of Egyptology and a renowned scholar.

McNamara describes the monument itself as a fascinating insight into the art and archaeology of ancient Sudan.“The new projection—and the scientific research behind it—will allow visitors to appreciate and understand the shrine’s original painted decoration like never before,” he adds

The project has been supported by James Lupton, the Ashmolean's chair of the board of visitors and his wife Béatrice. The projection onto the shrine will be free for all visitors to the Ashmolean’s Ancient Egypt and Sudan galleries, from 13 November.

#9562. The Ups and Downs of Communal Living

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

If you’re struggling with something, chances are the answer in some way, shape, or form is community. Or at least that’s been my experience in my 46 years on this too-often-lonely planet.

When I got confused about where to send my kid to school, I found a ragtag group of parents all over the country who were committed to being a force for integration. When I fell down the hell that is our elder care “system,” I found solace in day programs, support groups, and all other manner of collectivizing. And when I was pregnant and in my late 20s, trying to figure out how to be a grown-up, you better believe I jumped on the chance to live in intergenerational, interfaith cohousing with some intentional community veterans. I lived there for over a decade and it completely transformed how I understand abundance, cooperation, and, yes, the many uses of homegrown kale (true to stereotype).

So, of course, I am over the moon about a new anthology, Living, Together: Reimagining Community in the Age of Disconnection, just out from Beacon Press (who also published my book, Do It Anyway, back in the day). Living, Together features a few of my favorite contemporary thinkers on interdependence, including Rhaina Cohen (author of The Other Significant Others) and, as mentioned, Dani McClain.

Here’s an interview with the anthology’s editor, Samantha Paige Rosen.

Courtney Martin: You begin the book talking about your own pleasurable experience of living with your parents as an adult—something that grew out of crisis, but has become a choice. It seems that in the case of multigenerational households, part of the challenge is rewiring adult relationships and not falling back into early conditioning. How did you do this rewiring when you all lived together as adults?

Samantha Paige Rosen: For me and my parents, I think a handful of different things occurred. First, some of the rewriting began before I moved in with them. I lived with them for nine months when I was 24 after I returned from the East Coast and was considering a career shift. I stayed with them during the summers I was in graduate school for the next couple of years, and I did the same for most of my college summers. All that time, they were seeing the adult I’d become and I was seeing them with emerging young adult eyes. I think this cemented the adult-level friendship between us so that by the time I moved in at 29, after which I ended up staying for six years, we could build off of the rewiring we’d already done.

Another piece is communication. I love talking about my feelings and my perspective, and I want my loved ones to feel comfortable doing the same. So as much as my mother likes to joke that I talk everything to death—and I know I have to pick my moments; not everyone is receptive at every moment—I attribute the way we understand each other as adults to my communication skills and my parents’ openness to that, much of the time.

What that meant was that when there were instances over the six years I lived with my parents where my mom doted on me like she did when I was young, or my dad was a little too opinionated about my whereabouts, I could remind them, Thank you, I love you, and, as an adult, I’ve got this! If they’d make an assumption based on how I acted when I was younger, I’d call them out on it, nicely, and let them know that the thing they’re saying isn’t true of 30-something me. Of course, this goes both ways, and I let my parents know they could call me out, too. I worked hard to make sure I was seeing my parents as the fully realized adults they are and not just my mom and dad.

At the same time, I’ve always said that neither of my younger sisters could have lived with my parents as adults, but I obviously could. I don’t always need to be in charge, and I don’t mind a little doting! My sisters prefer to run the show and feel strongly about their independence. So perhaps there was an element of luck, personality-wise, too.

For readers who live in multigenerational households and have the difficulties around rewiring, I’d say tell and show your loved ones the ways you’ve changed—and often—and ask them to do the same. Communication is everything (and when that doesn’t work, demonstration is). And are there minor aspects of falling back into early conditioning that wouldn’t be so terrible to embrace?

CM: It seems like one of the biggest barriers for so many people to live more creatively and interdependently is cost. Cohousing, for example, is notoriously expensive to create and is still too elite a movement, as a result. What did you learn about the role that finances play in our ability to, as the subtitle says, reimagine community?

SPR: I relate to feeling priced out of communal living. I remember my college friend, Francesca, sending me this article about cohousing when I was at my most overwhelmed and depressed living alone, about six months before I ended up moving in with my parents. I had never heard of cohousing; she saw I needed communal living before I did. I remember feeling enraged, honestly, because she was like, “This is what you need!” and I felt like, Why did you make me aware of something I clearly needed but couldn’t afford?! The subtitle of the article was literally “Where Responsibilities Are Shared And Life Is A Little Less Lonely,” and I was so lonely, overworked, and just kind of crushed by the weight of life.

But a few weeks into living with my parents, I realized I was living communally, just in a different way. And now, I live alone in a townhouse and my parents live across the parking lot. We have dinner at least twice a week, we share groceries, we pet-sit for each other; I take my cat there in a backpack every day to play with their cats. Some people might say I live alone, and in some ways I do, but I can still reap some benefits of communal living in an informal way and that I can afford.

I’m not going to pretend that finances don’t offer access, or at least a wider ability to reimagine community. But only a few of the stories in Living, Together feature forms of intentional community that can have a high price for entry, like cohousing. That’s by design: I wanted readers to feel like they had many different models for getting their needs around communal living, and even community outside the home, met.

In the book, Amanda E. Machado and Rhaina Cohen both share stories of renting homes with friends, and Amanda’s essay, in particular, talks about the cost-sharing element of that approach. Essayist Elizabeth Hart Bergstrom lives in a separate space above their parents’ house, and Dani McClain shares the house she grew up in with her mother and daughter. Gabrielle Korn has a house with an attached studio apartment she rents out, and also offers for free to writers seeking short residencies.

Suanne Carlson shares a glimpse into the nomadic life, which I think more people are going to be forced to do if this housing crisis continues; for Suanne, living out of a vehicle is a choice that allows her to travel, feel at home in nature, and get together with other nomads who see home and community the way she does. Tiffany Harris writes about how she made a career out of how much she liked having roommates by supporting programming for Jewish people in their 20s who want to share living space and traditions with other young Jewish people. Simone Gorrindo writes about having an interdependent relationship with a neighbor when they were both new military wives and were incredibly lonely.

All of these forms of communal living have pluses and minuses. There’s no perfect way to live, and when you’re interdependent with others, there will always be friction. If you want the kind of communal living where you have completely separate space from other people, then, yes, it could be more expensive. (Although not necessarily: tiny house communities? Fourplexes? Accessory dwelling units? Separate apartments on the same floor as loved ones?) But there are so many other ways to live communally if you think outside formal intentional communities and realize you can…make up whatever you want!

[Here are some resources on making cohousing more affordable.]

CM: What was the biggest surprise of working on this anthology?

SPR: Working on the anthology further broadened the way I defined communal living.

I really have come to believe that communal living is any way a person is regularly interdependent with others around their home base, sharing time, resources, and offering a sense of safety.

Maybe it’s several generations of a family living within walking distance to one another, or neighbors who deliberately make time to see each other most days, share groceries or meals, and offer rides to doctors’ appointments. But to me, communal living is less about the roof you have over your head and more about how intentionally interdependent you are with others.

Reading the Q&A with Hank Gamel and Fran Biederman in Living, Together, where Fran, who is 91, talks about all the different ways she and her neighbor support each other got me thinking about this. So did Kristen Arnett and Simone Gorrindo’s essays. Kristen’s friends, her chosen family, all live within a short drive from each other. They celebrate every milestone together and jump at the chance to offer help, like inviting those who don’t have power during hurricane season to the house of whoever does. Simone’s neighbor taught her how to drive and helped Simone furnish her house. For a period of time, they had regular dinners, watched each other’s kids, and Simone even slept at her neighbor’s house on anxious nights while their husbands were deployed.

CM: What is one thing you have changed in your own life because of reading this book? A new tradition with your parents? A new way of using space?

SPR: I’ve become more flexible about the way I think about home, community, and my own future. As I write in my introduction to the book, I bought pretty hard into the American dream as a kid, including the idea of a “forever home.” I think I was seeking a feeling of safety, and the finality of a “forever home” seemed to offer that. But reading my contributors’ stories, seeing their openness to different configurations of housing and home, and the way those changed as their needs did over time, has taken the pressure off of finding that one ideal living scenario. I no longer feel like I’m searching for a place to settle; I just feel more settled within myself.

And it couldn’t have happened at a better time, because home and housing is so tenuous now for so many of us.

It feels freeing to have my attitude be that right now I live in a two-bedroom townhouse across the parking lot from my parents. It meets a lot of my needs, but not all of them. And when I’m missing having people in my immediate space, or there’s another reason this doesn’t work as well anymore, I tell myself that this living scenario can be for me until it isn’t. When my needs change, I can adapt to them. Someday, I hope to live close to a bunch of artists who also raise kids communally, in whatever form of housing that takes. But not today, and that’s fine!

This Q&A is republished from Courtney Martin’s Substack newsletter, Examined Family. Read the original newsletter.

#9560. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).
