#9559. Eight Fun Ways to Keep Your Summer Alive

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Backpack-and-pencil time is just about here, but it’s not too late to treat yourself to a healthy dose of summer joy.   There’s no need to feel bad about stretching that vacation feeling out as long as you can. These eight mini-vacations for the mind and spirit require no suitcases to pack (and unpack), no expensive gas tanks to fill, and no big credit card bills to pay. Not only are many of our favorite summery luxuries simple and inexpensive, research suggests they just might be good for us, too. Before you swap the flip-flops and tanks for boots and sweaters, take a moment to seize some feel-good fun.

You don’t need expensive tickets to the hottest concerts of the summer to reap the happy rewards of listening to live music. “Collective effervescence”—the feeling of meaning and closeness with others that we experience in a positive group activity—is key to a concert’s feel-good benefits, researchers say. While listening to songs at home is fun, too, the “sacredness and connection” of collective effervescence is rooted in the togetherness of a crowd at a concert, and the uplift can continue for as long as a week after.

Free and cheap local live music options abound in many areas, whether it’s an old-time swing band in the gazebo in the park, a vocalist on the patio at a nearby café, or a full orchestra playing to a grassy outdoor amphitheater. Bring a blanket, let the kids run if you’ve got any, and soak in that sweet collective effervescence.

A beach or lake vacation may not be in the plans this summer, but you can still treat yourself to a walk next to a stream or a paddle in a nearby pond.

Research finds that people who regularly spend time in natural environments like parks, woods, and beaches tend to have better physical and psychological health, and water offers specific benefits to well-being. According to new research from 19 countries, water-centric “blue spaces” like rivers, lakes, and oceans bring us feelings of restoration, calm, and greater mental and emotional energy. Being near water is itself beneficial, but swimming or even wading boosts the restorative effects.

My own summer favorites are regular evening walks around a small local lake and—if I can make it work—getting out on a stand-up paddle board at least once a summer. Happiness!

Research on the benefits of nature has generally focused on daytime hours, but that’s beginning to change. Researchers have created a “night sky connected index” (NSCI) to measure the effects of outdoor time at night, especially looking up at the sky, and they found that people with a higher NSCI tend to have “greater mental well-being and happiness.” Looking at the night sky is also linked to feelings of awe, according to the same study, and experiencing awe can help reduce negative thinking and boost our happiness.

August is Perseids meteor shower time: Every year, across the Northern Hemisphere, thousands of meteors may be visible as they streak across the night sky. As a child, my siblings and I would often sleep in the backyard in mid-August and happily count meteors while we lay on our backs in our sleeping bags. My backyard sleeping days are behind me, but I admit that lately adulthood has been so busy that I haven’t even looked up at night. Time to find the magic again.

No matter what outdoor activity you choose, getting outside in green space specifically (even parks and street greenery count!) is beneficial. But you can boost your outdoor fun—and health—even more by inviting others to share a meal together. Recent research finds that eating with others makes people feel more happiness and less stress, pain, and sadness that day compared to days when they only eat alone.

You don’t have to host a dinner party or spring for an expensive restaurant meal. Greater Good reader Catherine Michaud shared her simple, satisfying summer recipe with us: “Find a local park with good shade trees. Bring a book, a blanket, a friend (or three), lawn chairs, picnic, and board/lawn games.” Count us in.

Speaking of kids: As a kid of the 80s, I climbed countless trees with friends and siblings. But I am having trouble remembering a time when my own kids clambered up branches just to see how high they could go.

A recent Australian paper reviewed many studies about adventurous play and “overwhelmingly” concluded that children engaging in risky outdoor play showed better overall mental health and social abilities and were less prone to anxiety. “Risky outdoor play” generally includes activities involving high speeds or heights, play with dangerous tools (saws, knives) or near dangerous elements (fire, water, cliffs), rough-and-tumble play, and activities in which the child could “disappear” out of adult sight. This list may make some of us (including me) a little nervous, but maybe we could at least let the kids help build, light, and tend the fire for some late summer s’mores?

Articles and podcast episodes to help you find joy, laughter, and rest this summer.

The authors of the study specifically caution against helicopter parenting; it’s key, they say, that the kids learn to evaluate risks themselves. This isn’t a permission slip for parents to neglect safety, but it is a reminder that this summer it’s OK for parents to turn down the worry-meter, skip the hovering, and instead sit on the patio with a book or a friend while the kids take in a joyful climb or a bike race down the driveway.

This year’s World Cup excitement is over, but the sporting fun doesn’t need to end: People who watch sports, either live or on TV, tend to show a number of health benefits.

A new study published in the journal Nature found that watching live sports reduces the stress hormone cortisol and increases the social-bonding hormone oxytocin. So, whether it’s an evening of Little League or the Big Leagues, and whether you’re in the middle of a cheering crowd or cozied up on the couch during a thunderstorm, take a break from the end-of-summer rush and relax into a game, win or lose.

Greater Good reader and mom Aja Russo loves taking her kids strawberry picking every year in early summer. But if you missed strawberry picking time, and you didn’t plant a garden this year (raising my own hand), it’s not too late. Start reaping the benefits of gardening at a pick-your-own farm. Research finds that even short periods of gardening can lead to feeling calmer and more relaxed.

What to pick? Peach picking is still going strong in many areas, and apples aren’t just for autumn—popular varieties are ready for picking in August in much of the United States. If the climate where you live doesn’t cooperate with picking fruit right now, you can still exercise your green thumb and boost well-being by tending a plant indoors.

Yes, we said what we said. Most of us intuitively know that eating ice cream makes us feel good, but researchers were surprised when decades of observation found a lower rate of cardiovascular disease among diabetic people who ate a small amount (about half a cup) of ice cream a few times a week compared to diabetic people who never ate ice cream.

Now, scientists caution that this doesn’t mean that ice cream is a health food, but it certainly suggests that we don’t need to heap a topping of guilt onto our occasional cool treats. There’s still plenty of summertime left for a sunset trip to the local ice cream parlor with friends or family. Yum!

If you live in a place where the autumn chill will soon set in, now is prime time to revel in long evenings, soft temperatures, and as much summer well-being as you can seize. As the famous song goes, “Summertime, and the living is easy.” And healthy!

Sharon Holbrook is a writer and editor who has been published in the New York Times, Washington Post, and many other national and local publications. She lives with her family near Cleveland, Ohio.

#9557. Christie’s first Abu Dhabi art auction makes $8.9m

Christie's first Abu Dhabi fine art auction, held at The Edition Abu Dhabi

Christie’s first fine-art auction in Abu Dhabi has realised more than $8.9m, with several works fetching six figures and surpassing their original estimates.

The auction, titled Mawasim, was held last week (1 November) at The Abu Dhabi Edition. It marked the 20th anniversary of Christie’s first auction in the United Arab Emirates.

Topping the sale was Variations on the Hexagon (2006) by Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian. The work was estimated between $150,000 and $250,000. It sold for $844,800, after almost seven minutes of bidding.

The mirror mosaic panel was commissioned for the opening of the Jameel Gallery at the Victoria and Albert Museum.

“It is a magnificent work of exceptional historical significance,” said Ridha Moumni, chairman of Christie’s Middle East and Africa.

“Farmanfarmaian is undoubtedly one of the most talented female artists in the region. This particular work, however, is especially spectacular.”

Other works that led the sale included Fahrelnissa Zeid’s Composition (1948-1949), which fetched $524,800. Her Endless Thoughts, painted in the late 1970s, sold for $486,400.

Ali Banisadr’s Homo Deus (2018), meanwhile, sold for $512,000, as did Faisel Laibi Sahi’s Baghdad Café (The Coffee Shop) (2016), which set a record for the artist. The painting, which measures six metres in length, is the largest by the Iraqi painter to go under the hammer.

Mahmoud Saïd’s Portrait de Princesse Fadia (Portrait of Princess Fadia)(1952) was sold for $486,400. Paul Guiragossian’s Noces (Wedding), an oil-on-masonite work created between 1958 and 1959, fetched $486,400. The sale marked a record for the medium for the artist, as did Samia Halaby’s Yesterday (1978), which sold for $358,400. The painting is a prime example of Halaby’s work from the 70s, when she developed her idiosyncratic approach to geometric abstraction.

Overall, Christie’s announced nine auction records, including for Jellal Ben Abdallah, whose Les Musiciennes (The Female Musicians) (1973) sold for $204,800 against an estimate between $100,000 and $150,000. Juliana Seraphim’s Femme Fleur (Flower Woman) (1973) also set a record, selling for $83,200. It had been estimated between $25,000 and $35,000.

Mawasim also marked the auction debut for several artists, including Nabil Kanso, Rami Farook, Fatma Lootah and Afra Al Dhaheri.

Moumni said that the fine-art auction of modern and contemporary works from the Middle East and North Africa was “the strongest results since 2015.

“It sends a very strong signal to the market and underscores the growing demand for art from the [region],” he said. “The results also demonstrate the significant presence of artists of Iranian origin in the market. We witnessed particularly spirited bidding for these artists, which was very exciting to see.”

Works by Emirati artists, such as Najat Makki and Hassan Sharif, have also “performed exceptionally well,” Moumni said.

Makki’s Emirates of Love (2025) sold for $28,160, whereas a painting from Sharif’s celebrated Press Conference series sold for $83,200.

“We were delighted to see works by all these UAE artists supported by both local and international collectors,” Moumni said. “There is still work to be done in further developing their market value, but the results were a truly wonderful surprise and a testament to the vitality of the UAE’s creative art scene.”

The auction, Moumni said, attracted a “healthy mix” of private collectors and institutional buyers. Interestingly, 30 per cent of participants were Generation Z and the millennial generations. There were also several first-time bidders.

“Thirty-seven per cent of participants were new to Christie’s, representing an encouraging expansion of our collector base,” Moumni said.

Sunday’s auction was the climactic conclusion to a week-long exhibition at The Abu Dhabi Edition, which presented the works featured in the Mawasim auction. The works came from private as well as institutional collections, such as from the Dalloul Collection and the Trad family collection in Beirut and the Barjeel Art Foundation in Sharjah.

Christie’s first auction in the UAE was held in 2006 in Dubai, at a time when the city’s arts scene was at a pivotal moment. New galleries and institutions were opening up and the city was preparing to host the DIFC Gulf Art Fair, which would then be rebranded at Art Dubai.

As a 20th anniversary auction, Mawasim was held in Abu Dhabi during a similar landmark moment. The UAE capital is preparing to host its first Frieze in November and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is meanwhile gearing up for its December opening.

“It was particularly important for us to present this anniversary auction here in Abu Dhabi, a city that is home to some of the region’s most significant museums, with several more important cultural institutions set to open in the coming years.”

#9556. When Scientists Admit Mistakes, That Means Science Is Working

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When the first cases of COVID-19 were discovered in a hospital in Wuhan, I had already studied the U.S. public health response to seven epidemics and pandemics. I am no stranger to the role of politics in pandemic response. Still, the recent Senate hearings grilling Dr. Anthony Fauci alarmed me.

Fauci is a physician and immunologist who served as the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and as chief medical advisor to President Trump during the period of Covid-19—who has subsequently become a scapegoat for those who didn’t like the restrictions that came with the pandemic. As Senator Rand Paul put it, based on the evidence-free conspiracy theory that Dr. Fauci funded research that led to the pandemic: “One million Americans died from COVID and not even an apology from Dr. Anthony Fauci.”

While we might recognize such claims as preposterous, it would be a mistake to treat these hearings as mere political theater. Those who are treating errors in the understanding of Covid-19 as criminal threaten one of the most important public goods we have during an infectious disease crisis: the willingness of experts to publicly admit mistakes.

Dr. Fauci has openly acknowledged missteps, communication errors, and evolving judgments in responding to the COVID-19 pandemic—an honesty that is not matched by his critics. Instead, his honesty has been leveraged by them to sow doubt in science itself.

But the reason we turn to experts during a crisis is not because they are omniscient. Of course they aren’t. It is because they learn faster and better than non-experts. Learning, however, is a naturally error-prone process. And learning when a novel infectious disease is fueling a global pandemic is particularly so. One can hope that scientists responding to such a crisis will be able to reduce uncertainties in a linear and predictable fashion. But that is not the norm.

As a social scientist, if I discover something new, when I present my findings to my colleagues, the most likely result is that they will tell me all the ways they think I might be wrong. My job is to prove that my findings hold even after considering their counterarguments. Skepticism is essential in the process of separating fact from fiction. We have more confidence in results that have survived such pressure-testing.

Experts at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) during the pandemic received just this type of skepticism from other experts. And yet much of the political commentary surrounding these normal and essential controversies cited the evidence of controversy as proof the CDC was flailing.

This approach treats science as though the discovery of new facts unfolds like a treasure hunt where the first person to find the treasure opens the lid and everyone can see the treasure with their own eyes. In a treasure hunt, discovery and validation are essentially the same thing.

But science does not work this way. Take the discovery of HIV. Dr. Luc Montaignier identified the virus under an electron microscope in February 1983. Uncertainty surrounding whether the virus was causative or opportunistic led to more than a year of additional research, culminating in four papers published by Dr. Robert Gallo and his colleagues in 1984, that affirmed Montaignier’s finding. According to Montaignier, it was one of these publications, in particular, that “convinced the scientific community that this new retrolentivirus was the cause of AIDS.”

This example shows something that is true across the sciences. New discoveries that eventually become accepted as scientific facts can linger for an extended period as mere “claims” while uncertainties are addressed.

Critics argue that the scientific uncertainty around the discovery of the AIDS virus was unnecessarily prolonged and cost lives. If moving quickly on yet-to-be-validated evidence is the right approach during a pandemic, note that Fauci and his public health colleagues are currently being attacked for doing exactly that. Public health experts believed at the outset that COVID-19 was like SARS, with transmission most likely to occur late in the course of infection. Hence the guidance that directed the public and health care workers to wear masks when caring for patients already showing symptoms. Mounting evidence of asymptomatic infection eventually proved that COVID-19 transmission was very different from SARS, leading to new masking guidance.

When should public health experts act on early, but unvalidated, evidence versus taking the time to iron out uncertainties? While it may look obvious in hindsight, there is no magic formula that can sort out in advance when the better course will have been to slow down and validate versus act on plausible, but still uncertain, claims.

Climate scientists would almost certainly never argue their experience in the public eye has been a picnic. But they had one big advantage over those trying to guide the response to a pandemic driven by a novel infectious disease. Climate scientists had decades—as opposed to only weeks or days—to conduct research before they were asked to explain what they knew to the public. In fact, climate scientists did not always expect warming to result from burning fossil fuels. Up until the 1950s, the prevailing wisdom was that the oceans would absorb excess carbon dioxide so that there would be minimal if any warming. Roger Revelle and Hans Seuss, who together discovered the error, both received awards for their research.

When a novel infectious disease comes to town, the first cases detected are rarely the actual start of the outbreak. There are no tests to make a positive diagnosis. Some of the suspected cases turn out to have other causes. People who are infected are overlooked. Data collected at the outset is patchy and error-prone. As the public health community pivots to emergency response footing, they begin to collect data more systematically. Even so, new data can rapidly overturn early assumptions. The case definition for COVID-19 was updated almost weekly during the first 10 weeks of the pandemic.

Monday morning quarterbacking is easy. Try advising countries on how to manage a growing pandemic while the ground is moving beneath your feet.

As the United States’ performance during the COVID-19 pandemic is reviewed, even those who are not engaging in political grandstanding tend to reduce the effort to a scorecard that tallies the times experts were right versus the times they were wrong. Even if the reversals are few in number, they are barely tolerated. We usually give examinations to people after they have had time to learn and master the material. What is the right metric to use for public health experts who are trying to inform us when the answers are still being discovered?

Speaking of treasure, I think we were lucky during COVID-19 to have public health experts who were willing to admit mistakes as soon as they were discovered. Things will go markedly worse for us if, during the next pandemic, they are less forthcoming.

An earlier version of this article first appeared on MS NOW.

Ann Keller, Ph.D., is an associate professor of health politics & policy at UC Berkeley School of Public Health.

#9555. What is a circadian rhythm disorder? Plus, 6 ways to treat it

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You’re tired when you should be awake, or wired when you should be asleep. Whether it’s 2am and you’re staring at the ceiling, your body still hasn’t recovered from that red-eye flight, or the night shift is taking its toll, the struggle is the same: your internal clock and your life are pulling in opposite directions.

These are circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs), and they happen when your body's sleep-wake cycle doesn't match your daily schedule. And they're more common than you'd think — often mistaken for stress or brushed off as one more thing to deal with once life slows down.

The good news is that CRSDs are medically recognized and treatable. Below, we’ll cover the different types, why they happen, and how to get your sleep back on track.

Your body has an internal clock—the circadian rhythm—that regulates when you feel sleepy and when you feel alert. It runs on roughly a 24-hour cycle, shaped by external cues like light, temperature, and meal timing.

A circadian rhythm sleep disorder (CRSD) occurs when your internal clock consistently falls out of sync with your environment, social schedule, or desired sleep times.

There are several distinct types of circadian rhythm sleep disorders:

Delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD): Sleep comes much later than usual (often in the early hours of the morning) followed by a struggle to wake up on time.

Advanced sleep phase disorder (ASPD): Sleep arrives early in the evening, and waking happens in the early hours of the morning — the reverse of DSPD.

Non-24-hour sleep-wake disorder: Sleep and wake times drift later or earlier each day instead of settling into a 24-hour rhythm. This pattern is most common in people who are blind.

Irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder: Sleep is broken into several short stretches across the day and night, without a clear pattern.

Shift work disorder: Night or rotating shift schedules conflict with the body's natural sleep timing.

Jet lag disorder: A temporary misalignment between the body’s internal clock and local time after crossing time zones.

Symptoms vary based on the type of CRSD, but the core issue is the same: sleep happens at the wrong time.

trouble falling asleep at a normal bedtime

difficulty waking up in the morning, or waking too early

mood changes, including irritability, anxiety, or low mood

Circadian rhythm sleep disorders often stem from multiple factors at once, ranging from lifestyle and environment to biology.

Light exposure: Light entering your eyes is the strongest external cue for your internal clock to stay in sync with the outside world. Too much bright light at night, like from screens, or too little natural light in the morning can push your clock in the wrong direction.

Genetics: Your genes can set your natural sleep timing earlier or later than average. Certain gene variants have been linked to differences in circadian timing, which may explain a lifelong tendency toward being a night owl or an early riser.

Age: Your sleep timing usually changes with age. Teenagers drift toward later sleep and wake times, while older adults often feel tired earlier in the evening and wake earlier as a result.

Shift work and irregular schedules: Night or rotating shifts keep you awake when your body expects to be asleep. Irregular eating and exercise can add to that disruption.

Neurological conditions: Conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, or a history of traumatic brain injury are tied to a higher risk of circadian disruption, including fragmented or irregular sleep. Researchers are still working out whether disrupted rhythms are a cause, an early sign, or both.

Blindness: Without light entering the eyes, the brain's clock loses its main external cue for staying aligned with a 24-hour day.

No matter which type of CRSD you're dealing with, you can get your internal clock back on track. Here's what works, and how to find the right approach for you.

In the morning: Bright daylight early in the day helps advance your clock, which is especially useful for delayed sleep phase disorder. During darker months, using a bright light therapy box (10,000 lux) for 20–30 minutes after waking can substitute for sunlight. If you have any eye conditions, it's a good idea to check with a doctor before starting.

In the evening: Reduce bright light 2–3 hours before bed to ease your body into sleep mode. Screens and overhead lighting can suppress melatonin production, while dimmer, warmer light helps your body settle down.

Traveling across time zones? The strategy for beating jet lag with light depends on which direction you're flying. Seek bright light in the new morning and avoid it in the new evening when flying east. Do the reverse when flying west. A day or two of light timing can speed up your adjustment.

💙 Pair your morning light with a Morning Meditation from the Daily Calm.

One of the most effective ways to steady your circadian rhythm is to maintain a regular sleep schedule. Wake up at the same time every day—even on weekends—to give your body a consistent cue to work with. It may feel hard at first, but with consistency, your body naturally adjusts to the rhythm.

Working nights or rotating shifts? "Consistent" doesn't have to mean conventional. Try anchoring your sleep to the same block of hours on workdays, and limiting how far you drift on days off.

💙 Build a sleep routine with Making Progress from the 7 Days of Sleep series on Calm.

Chronotherapy involves slowly adjusting your sleep and wake times in one direction, a little each day, until you reach your target schedule.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? This might mean going to bed a few hours later each day (moving all the way around the clock) until you land on your desired bedtime. It's a demanding process, and there's some risk of your schedule drifting further off track, so it's best done under a sleep specialist's guidance rather than on your own.

A sleep specialist can help tailor chronotherapy to your specific pattern.

Sleep difficulties often come with anxiety about sleep itself, which can make it harder to fall asleep. Mindfulness practices can help calm your racing mind and relieve that anxiety. Even a few minutes of mindful breathing or a short guided meditation can quiet your mind enough to help you drift off.

💙 Try this Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

Melatonin is a hormone your brain produces, and its levels naturally rise in the evening — signaling to your body that sleep time is approaching. Think of a melatonin supplement as a timing tool rather than a sedative that will help you fall asleep on the spot.

Dealing with delayed sleep phase disorder? Take a low dose (around 0.5–3 mg) three hours before your desired bedtime to help adjust your clock gradually. A doctor or sleep specialist can advise on the right amount for your situation.

Traveling across time zones? Melatonin taken around your target bedtime (about an hour before) in the new time zone is a well-supported way to adjust to jet lag faster.

💙 Discover the best time to take melatonin for restful sleep.

For persistent or severe circadian rhythm sleep disorders, professional support can make a real difference. A sleep specialist may recommend a formal evaluation, actigraphy (a wrist sensor that tracks sleep-wake patterns over time), or a combination of treatments.

Struggling with non-24-hour or irregular sleep-wake rhythm disorder? These patterns respond less predictably to light and schedule changes on their own. A sleep specialist can build a plan around your specific pattern.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is also sometimes paired with circadian-focused treatments. It’s a structured therapy that targets the thoughts and habits keeping you awake.

Several everyday habits can throw off your circadian rhythm, including irregular sleep schedules, shift work, jet lag, too much screen use at night, and inconsistent light exposure. Stress, alcohol, caffeine, and some medications can also throw off your body's timing.

Some circadian rhythm sleep disorders can go away on their own, but it depends on the type you're dealing with. Jet lag usually clears up within a few days as your body adjusts to a new time zone. But most chronic circadian rhythm sleep disorders don't resolve without changes to your sleep schedule, light exposure, or daily habits. The sooner you start addressing it, the more manageable the shift becomes.

Not quite, though circadian rhythm sleep disorder and insomnia can feel similar. Insomnia is trouble falling or staying asleep, no matter the time of day. A circadian rhythm sleep disorder is sleep happening at the wrong time. Someone with delayed sleep phase disorder, for example, might sleep just fine from 3am to 11am, instead of a more typical schedule.

The time it takes to reset your circadian rhythm depends on how far your body clock has shifted. Jet lag typically settles within a few days, but a significantly delayed or advanced sleep schedule can take several weeks of consistent habit changes to correct. Light therapy and melatonin can speed the process along, but there's no quick fix.

Melatonin can help with circadian rhythm sleep disorders, but the timing matters. For delayed sleep phase disorder, a low dose taken several hours before your target bedtime can help shift your clock gradually. For jet lag, taking it closer to your target bedtime tends to work better. A doctor or sleep specialist can help you figure out the right dose and timing for your situation.

If your sleep schedule has been getting in the way of work, relationships, or daily life—and adjusting your habits hasn’t helped—it's worth reaching out to a doctor or sleep specialist. They can assess whether you have a circadian rhythm sleep disorder and recommend a treatment plan.

💙 Learn more about the 7 most common sleep disorders.

In many cases, you can fix your circadian rhythm naturally. Focus on getting bright light in the morning and keeping consistent sleep and wake times. For milder patterns, these changes alone can make a noticeable difference, though more serious cases may need extra support.

#9554. This Vitamin Reduces Depression Symptoms By 50%

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

Taking a high dose of vitamin B6 for a month reduced depression symptoms in people already experiencing them.

The vitamin helps the brain produce chemical messengers involved in mood regulation.

The findings suggest a potential role for B6 in treating depression, although larger clinical trials are needed.

Almost 270 adults, mostly young women, took part in the research.

They were randomly assigned to take either 100 mg of vitamin B6, vitamin B12 or a placebo each day for around a month.

Among almost 60 people with at least mild depression symptoms at the start, those taking B6 improved more than those receiving B12 or a placebo.

Average depression scores fell by about 54 percent in the symptomatic B6 group, compared with 24 percent in the placebo group.

The benefit remained after accounting for differences in how severe their symptoms had been at the start.

The findings come from a new analysis of data collected in the same research programme that previously reported reduced anxiety after B6 supplementation.

Vitamin B6 supports several processes involved in regulating mood.

Dr David Field, the study’s first author, said:

“Vitamin B6 plays a crucial role in the production of several chemical messengers in the brain, including serotonin and GABA, both of which are central to mood regulation.”

GABA helps restrain nerve cell activity, contributing to the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain.

Increasing B6 availability could boost their production, potentially explaining the improvement in depression symptoms.

Inflammation may also play a role, potentially affecting both depression and how the body uses B6.

Vitamin B6 occurs naturally in foods including poultry, fish, chickpeas, bananas and fortified cereals.

However, the trial tested a high supplement dose, rather than a change in everyday food intake.

High doses of B6 can cause peripheral nerve damage, so the researchers say supplementation at these doses requires medical supervision.

Larger trials now need to establish the most effective dose, monitor safety and determine whether B6 could help alongside existing depression treatments.

The study was published in the journal Depression and Anxiety (Field et al., 2026).

#9553. Do You Compare Yourself to Your Partner? It’s Not All Bad

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

After venturing through the wasteland of modern dating, it would be natural to harbor disdain for social comparison. Dating apps require you to stand out, which means you can’t just be yourself; you need to sell yourself as more appealing than the 50,000 sexy singles in your area. Putting yourself on display and knowing you’re being compared to others can feel exhausting. But once you’ve swiped right, matched, and established a lasting romantic relationship, surely the social comparisons are all in the rearview mirror…right?

That couldn’t be further from the truth. Research suggests we compare ourselves to romantic partners more than anyone else in our lives—on average several times per day. In my own studies, I’ve endeavored to unpack these daily partner comparisons to understand: What kinds of people make partner comparisons, and why? The answer, it seems, depends on the type of comparisons partners are making: either based on our unique abilities, or on the opinions we hold. The good news: Comparisons can offer a learning opportunity and even bring us closer together as partners.

Many partner comparisons revolve around who is better at a given activity—also known as “ability-based comparisons.” These comparisons can range from trivial (Who’s the better bowler?) to weighty (Who’s the better parent?).

In my latest study with collaborators Robin Edelstein and Stephen Garcia, we studied patterns in who makes more of these ability-based comparisons. We surveyed over 1,100 U.S. adults in romantic relationships, asking them questions about how regularly they compare themselves to their partners. For instance, one question asked them, “To what extent do you pay a lot of attention to how you do things relative to how your significant other does things?” Participants also completed measures of self-esteem, relationship quality, and demographics.

The results were clear: People who were younger, those with lower self-esteem, and those in shorter and less satisfying relationships were particularly likely to make ability-based comparisons. Men in relationships with men also reported making more of these comparisons than any other gender pairing, but we only surveyed 37 men in same-gender relationships, so take this finding with a grain of salt.

A second type of comparison involves comparing judgments and attitudes—known as “opinion-based comparisons.” In these comparisons, people evaluate their own opinions by comparing with those of their partners. For instance, before enthusiastically locking in a major purchase, a partner might wonder, “Would my partner consider this a good deal, too?” Similar considerations may arise in the contexts of voting, child care, or anywhere judgments lead to decisions.

When it came to who was most prone to making opinion-based comparisons, our results flipped: These were most common among people in longer and more satisfying relationships.

Taken together, these individual characteristics paint two portraits of people who frequently compare themselves to their partners.

The first portrait is that of a young, insecure partner who is in a newer relationship and unsure whether that relationship will work out. Think Bella Swan from Twilight who worries endlessly about whether Edward is too good for her. And, indeed, when we asked participants why they made partner comparisons, two of their motives included assessing equity and predicting the relationship’s trajectory. For instance, participants grappled with questions like, “Am I doing for her as she is doing for me?”

The second portrait is that of someone in a long-term relationship who respects the knowledge and expertise of their partner and seeks to harness it as a tool for growth and decision making. For this one, think Leslie Knope from Parks and Rec who regularly compares her own judgments to those of her long-term work wife, Ann Perkins, as a means to make better decisions. This theme, too, emerged from our participants. For instance, one participant lovingly wrote about how his partner outshines him in most areas, and this dynamic continually inspires him to grow.

Yet partner comparison isn’t limited to these two portraits. Whereas these portraits describe those who compare most frequently, we found most people make some comparisons sometimes. What motivates occasional comparers?

The two most common motives for partner comparison were striving to gain a deeper understanding of oneself and one’s partner. With respect to self-evaluation, one participant shared that they compare regularly to their partner because comparison helps them benchmark their progress toward goals. Want to know if your cooking class has paid off? One of the best ways to evaluate your growth is to see if your latest dish can delight your family in the same way that your partner’s cooking always does.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Partner comparisons can also help us understand our partners’ quirks, what we call partner evaluation. For instance, one participant shared how she compares her upbringing to that of her partner, which helps her understand why her partner thinks, feels, and behaves so differently than she does.

It’s no secret that social comparison can sting. No parent wants to hear, “I like Mom better,” and no newlywed wants to hear, “How did you land such a catch?” We find in our studies that partner comparisons are often involuntarily thrust upon people who would have preferred not to be compared. It can be true what they say, “Comparison is the thief of joy.”

But comparison does more than push our emotional buttons. Partner comparisons help us assess our relationship and calibrate our behavior, such as how we divide household labor. They allow us to make important decisions, like who should take ownership over responsibilities. They serve as sources of growth, and they teach us about ourselves and our partners.

Comparing yourself to your partner isn’t necessarily a sign that something’s wrong. Rather, partner comparison can be a handy strategy for making sense of your social world. The key is to use it as a tool that stays in its place, rather than letting it undermine your self-worth or relationship.

Serena D’souza contributed to this article.

Zachary Reese, Ph.D., is an assistant professor of psychology at the University of San Francisco where he directs the Love and Communication Lab. He received his undergraduate degree in psychology from Goucher College in 2016 and his Ph.D. in social psychology from the University of Michigan in 2022.

#9552. Body doubling: what it is, how it works, and tips to try

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

If you’ve ever opened your laptop to begin your workday from home or checked your mountain of a to-do list and felt zero motivation to tackle it, you’re in good company. On days that you just can’t find the energy or focus to get started, it can help to have a little boost of accountability.

Body doubling, a phrase that means working alongside another person, has gained popularity over the years and is especially popular among people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Body doubling (either in person or virtually) is said to help motivate people to stay focused and accountable for the tasks at hand. And while it isn’t a formal treatment or backed by robust clinical research, plenty of people have spoken to its effectiveness.

So, what does body doubling involve, and why do so many people swear by it? More importantly, will it work for you? Pull up a seat and let’s explore what you need to know about the technique, plus a few simple ways to try it out for yourself.

Body doubling is the practice of working alongside another person to stay focused and complete a task, either in the same space or virtually. According to the ADDA, the term “body doubling” was coined in the late 1990s by ADHD coach Linda Anderson.

The rationale behind body doubling is that having someone else present and engaged in their own task can make it easier to start and stay on track with yours. To be clear, there’s no coaching or collaboration involved. You’re just working next to each other, because a shared presence can create a sense of structure and accountability.

If you sit at your kitchen table while your roommate does homework, join a silent Zoom session where everyone works on their own projects, or even fold laundry while a friend cleans their space on FaceTime, those are all examples of body doubling.

Many people feel that body doubling helps them break through procrastination and maintain momentum,  especially during overwhelming tasks.

Getting started: Sometimes the hardest part is just beginning. Having someone else nearby can help create a sense of gentle urgency.

Staying on task: When another person is focused, it can be easier for you to stay engaged with your own work.

Feeling less isolated: This practice can reduce the emotional friction that builds when you’re feeling alone in your head.

Creating structure: Knowing someone will be present at a specific time gives your day a natural rhythm. Plus, it can add a layer of accountability.

This technique has gained popularity within the ADHD community. While it’s important to note that this isn’t a clinically recommended treatment—and there’s limited research to support it—many people with ADHD do say that it helps them function more consistently. The idea is that having someone nearby provides external structure and co-regulation.

When your executive functioning is impaired, simple tasks can feel overwhelming. But body doubling creates a soft sense of accountability, which can make it easier to begin and stay engaged in tasks.

With that said, some people find it distracting or feel pressure to “perform,” especially if their partner’s energy doesn’t match theirs. Additionally, if your body double doesn’t understand ADHD, their presence can sometimes feel more frustrating than supportive.

If you’re navigating ADHD, body doubling could be another great tool to add to your toolkit. But only if it feels natural to you.

Disclaimer: Please note that body doubling isn’t a substitute for medication or therapy for people with ADHD.

If you find it hard to begin or stay engaged with tasks, body doubling could be the flexible tool you need. To get started, look for someone who matches your energy and who also makes you feel comfortable.

Here are nine ways you can mindfully add body doubling into your life.

If you’re new to body doubling, try it during something that feels manageable, like folding laundry or organizing your desk. This can give you space to experiment without the pressure of a high-stakes deadline or an environment that isn’t familiar to you, like a coworking space or coffee shop.

Have a quick conversation about what you both want. Ask the other person if you’ll talk, stay silent, or check in at the end.

Clear expectations help make the experience smooth and more supportive.

💙 Stay on the same page with your coworking partner with guidance from Jay Shetty’s Expectations.

Working alongside others in total silence can be helpful for concentrating and removing social pressure, while still giving you the benefits of shared presence.

Try scheduling a Zoom session where you say hello, then mute yourselves and work independently. You could also start a silent group video call with coworkers and only use the chat to check in.

If real-time body doubling feels overwhelming or isn’t accessible, consider searching for helpful videos on YouTube or TikTok.

Search for “study with me” or “body doubling,” and you’ll find creators who film themselves doing everyday tasks. By watching someone else stay focused, it may help you do the same.

Whether it’s a weekly Sunday cleaning hour with a friend or a daily Zoom session at 9am, a recurring slot can build structure into your routine. This can be especially helpful if you struggle with executive function challenges.

Related read: Meditation for ADHD: 9 tips and techniques

You and your body double don’t need to be doing the same thing. One of you could be writing emails while the other is meal prepping or baking a cake.

What matters most is that the energy feels aligned, focused, and respectful.

Related read: How to focus better: 8 tips to improve concentration

Make whatever task you’re doing as manageable as possible. Choose a specific task to start with, and try doing it for 15–30 minutes at first.

This reduces overwhelm and helps give you a clear finish line.

Some people feel vulnerable doing tasks in front of others, especially ones tied to shame or executive dysfunction.

So, choose a body double who won’t judge or try to fix you.

💙 Learn how to build relationships with people you trust during this Mindful Friendships session with Jay Shetty.

If you prefer asynchronous support, text a friend when you start a task and again when you finish. On the flip side, if you’re more motivated in groups, explore coworking in community accountability spaces.

Remember, there’s no one right way to body double. The key is to experiment and adjust based on what feels good to you.

Yes. Body doubling only needs one other person who is working at the same time as you. They can be in the room or on a video call. They don’t need to share your task or give you feedback.

Whether it works varies from person to person. Research on body doubling is limited, and many reports come from people who have tried it. Start with one short session and notice if it’s easier to begin and stay on task.

Body doubling works by providing subtle social accountability and structure. When another person is present, your brain registers the shift in environment. This presence can make it easier for you to start a task or stay with it.

And the accountability can be enough to kickstart momentum, especially if you’re someone who tends to overthink or avoid certain tasks.

It can. Procrastination often stems from overwhelm, perfectionism, and decision fatigue. But body doubling can add a sense of time and presence. You can see that there’s someone else there doing their own thing. And, as a result, it can become a little easier for you to start doing your own thing.

It allows the pressure of the task to lift, even though it may still feel hard.

There can be cons of body doubling. Some people find it distracting, especially if the other person wants to talk and you don’t. Additionally, if you have social anxiety or a history of trauma, being observed might make you feel emotionally charged.

In general, this practice isn’t for everyone. If you’re curious, check in with yourself. Ask if it’s something that would feel supportive and safe. If not, then it’s okay to step back and try a different format.

Anyone can try body doubling. While the term does have roots in ADHD communities, the technique can be applied to anyone. If you struggle with focus or motivation, this practice might be the thing for you.

Plus, if you’ve ever gotten more done in a coffee shop than at home, or felt a boost from working silently next to a friend, you’ve already experienced a version of body doubling.

You don’t need someone in the same room to try body doubling. Virtual options can be just as effective. You could join a coworking session on Zoom or even stream a “study with me” video in the background.

That being said, if you’d rather keep it low-contact, text a friend when you’re about to start a task. Then text them again when you finish. The key isn’t the format; it’s the feeling of shared effort and accountability. So, do whatever feels right to you.

#9550. How to deal with anxious-ambivalent attachment in a relationship

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Have you ever texted your partner only to spiral into oblivion waiting for them to respond? You wonder if they’re upset with you, if you did something wrong, or if they’re quietly pulling away. When their response finally comes through, you exhale the biggest sigh of relief. And then you start second-guessing why you were so worried in the first place.

If this sounds familiar, you may be dabbling in the world of ambivalent attachment, which is one of many attachment styles formed in adolescence and carried into adulthood.

Ambivalent attachment is a relationship pattern where you want to feel close to your partner but can’t always get there. It can show up as craving reassurance but doubting it, swinging between feeling connected to your partner and fearing they’ll leave, or analyzing small interactions for a hidden meaning that often isn’t there. While it may feel overwhelming, this attachment style isn’t a flaw in your personality, but rather a pattern shaped by early experiences in your life.

Let’s unpack what ambivalent attachment means, how to spot the signs in adulthood, and what to do if you (or your partner) lean toward this attachment style. Plus, we’ll dive into how to create steadier, more supportive relationships that feel good for all involved.

Anxious-ambivalent attachment—also called ambivalent attachment—is a relationship pattern where you crave reassurance yet struggle to feel settled once it’s given. It’s like wanting to lean on someone but worrying they might step away just as you do.

In adult relationships, ambivalent attachment may show up as feeling unsure about your partner’s commitment to you, cycling between connection and doubt, or getting caught in emotional highs and lows depending on how available your partner feels to you.

While it can feel overwhelming, this isn’t a flaw. It’s a protective strategy learned early in life that can be reshaped over time.

Ambivalent attachment often develops in childhood when caregiving is inconsistent. Basically, sometimes you were nurtured, and sometimes you weren’t. This unpredictability creates uncertainty in children, as they learn that comfort may arrive (but not reliably), so they cling tightly when it does appear. Over time, this wires the nervous system to stay on high alert for signs of loss or disconnection.

While it may seem easy to blame the caregivers involved, that’s not always the best answer or solution. Many people provide inconsistent care because of stress, lack of support, or their own attachment struggles. The good news is that even if this style formed early, it can shift in adulthood through consistent experiences of safety and connection.

Ambivalent attachment doesn’t always look dramatic from the outside. It often shows up in subtle, everyday ways that leave both partners feeling drained or confused. While everyone feels insecure at times, people with an ambivalent attachment style experience these patterns more intensely and more often.

1. Constant need for reassurance: You might ask for confirmation of your partner’s love or commitment regularly through words, texts, or gestures. The tricky part for people with an ambivalent attachment style is that reassurance often doesn’t stick. Even after hearing “I love you,” doubt can creep back quickly, fueling the cycle for reassurance again.

2. Fear of abandonment: Small shifts in a partner’s behavior—like if they take longer than usual to reply to a message or are quieter than usual—can trigger unnecessary worry. The fear isn’t just about being left by your partner, it’s about being forgotten or no longer valued. And for someone with this attachment style, those fears can be dire.

3. Hyper-attunement to signals: People with ambivalent attachment often read between the lines of every interaction, scanning tone, body language, or text punctuation for hidden meaning. A short text that simply says, “K,” might feel like rejection rather than just brevity.

4. Emotional highs and lows: Relationships can feel like a rollercoaster. You may feel ecstatic when things feel close and connected, then anxious when any distance appears. The intensity of these swings can feel overwhelming for both partners.

5. Difficulty trusting stability: Even when the relationship is going well, there’s a lingering sense that it could change at any moment. This makes it hard to relax into intimacy, because safety doesn’t feel fully reliable.

6. Feeling “too much” or “not enough”: Self-doubt often runs in the background, accompanied by persistent worrying that your needs are excessive or fearing that you’re somehow lacking. This inner tug-of-war can make it difficult to feel secure in how you show up in a relationship.

Working with ambivalent attachment is about finding steadier ground, both within yourself and your relationships. These strategies combine self-regulation, clearer communication, and practical agreements that build trust over time.

1. Recognize and name the pattern: The first step is simply noticing when old fears are coming up. Take time to put a name to the feeling, and remind yourself that it’s a learned response and not proof that something is wrong with you or your relationship. Taking a beat to give your feelings a name gives you the chance to pause before you react impulsively.

2. Soothe your body before your thoughts: Ambivalent attachment often activates the nervous system, which can make worries feel louder than they are. Simple grounding tools, such as intentional breathing, a mindful walk, or even running cold water over your wrists (which may help calm your nervous system) can bring your body back to baseline. Once you’re calmer, you’ll have more perspective on what’s really happening.

3. Ask directly instead of protesting: Protest behaviors (testing someone, withdrawing your affection, or sending a string of texts from the top of your mind) can backfire and push your partner away instead of bringing them closer. Practice naming your needs clearly instead. Try saying something like, “I’m feeling anxious right now and could use reassurance that we’re okay.” It might feel vulnerable to be so honest and open, but being direct usually leads to better connection.

4. Build a personal reassurance toolkit: Instead of depending only on your partner for reassurance, create a set of resources you can turn to yourself. This might include rereading kind messages, journaling, doing grounding exercises, or calling a supportive friend. Having options beyond your partner reduces the sense of desperation when anxiety spikes.

5. Practice small steps toward trust: Shifting attachment styles takes time, but small experiments help. Try waiting a little longer than you typically would before sending a check-in text, and see how that feels. You can also remind yourself of past experiences where closeness stood the test of time or survived a disagreement. Each successful moment builds evidence that security is possible, even if your old fears insist otherwise.

💙 Looking for tips to self-soothe? Try the Calming Anxiety guided practice on the Calm app.

6. Offer steady reassurance with boundaries: Consistency may help calm anxiety. Simple habits like a morning check-in or saying when you’ll call back create predictability. But it’s also important to pair reassurance with realistic boundaries. You might say, “I can’t text during work, but I’ll check in at lunch.”

7. Respond to the need, not just the words: Underneath protests or big reactions is usually a fear of being abandoned. Instead of focusing only on the tone or delivery of something your partner says, try reflecting the underlying need. You can say, “I hear that you’re worried I’m pulling away, but I want you to know I’m here.” This validation often matters more than a perfect solution.

8. Set clear repair practices: When tensions rise, agree in advance on how to pause and return to the conversation when you’re level-headed. Try saying, “If one of us feels overwhelmed, we’ll take a 20-minute break and come back at an agreed time.” Returning as promised helps rebuild trust, strengthens your relationship, and makes conflicts feel less threatening.

💙 Need a little more support? Check out the Kind Communication meditation on the Calm app.

9. Create shared routines for connection: Structure helps balance anxiety. A weekly check-in, an agreed-upon text during the workday, or even a daily hug ritual can anchor the relationship. These small but predictable moments reduce the need for constant reassurance.

Related read: How to use words of encouragement: 50 examples

10. Name the cycle and work as a team: Instead of blaming each other, talk about the pattern: “We tend to argue when I get quiet, and you seek more closeness. How can we catch it earlier?” Naming the cycle makes it something you face together, rather than a flaw in either partner.

💙 Learn how to take A Purposeful Pause with Jay Shetty on the Calm app.

Ambivalent attachment usually begins in early childhood. When a caregiver is sometimes warm and attentive but other times distracted, stressed, or unavailable, a child learns that love is unpredictable. This inconsistency creates anxiety about whether comfort will be there when it’s needed most.

Over time, the child develops strategies to cling tightly to connection, like seeking closeness while bracing for it to disappear. It’s not always about neglect. Often, caregivers themselves are overwhelmed or carrying their own attachment wounds. But the result is the same, and it’s that love is both essential and unreliable.

You may notice repeating patterns in your relationships, like craving reassurance but rarely feeling settled when you receive it. Small shifts in your partner’s tone, attention, or texting habits may trigger outsized worry about abandonment.

Overthinking, analyzing, or swinging between feeling deeply connected and then uncertain are also common. If these patterns show up across multiple relationships, that can be a strong sign of ambivalent attachment.

Attachment styles can change. While your early experiences lay the foundation, your attachment style can shift as you build new experiences of safety and stability. Supportive relationships, therapy, and personal work on self-regulation all help strengthen secure attachment.

The process is gradual and often happens through repeated moments of repair and reassurance. Over time, these experiences retrain your nervous system to trust that closeness can last.

Both ambivalent and avoidant attachment come from early inconsistencies in caregiving, but they lead to opposite coping strategies. People with ambivalent attachment often lean in, seeking closeness, reassurance, and connection. Sometimes, these manifest in ways that feel intense or overwhelming to their partner.

People with avoidant attachment tend to lean out. They value independence, minimize their needs, and withdraw when relationships feel too vulnerable. Ambivalent attachment is marked by fear of abandonment, while avoidant attachment is marked by discomfort with intimacy.

Yes, therapy can be effective. Working with an attachment-focused therapist gives you a consistent relationship where trust and stability are practiced week after week. Different forms of therapy like Emotionally Focused Therapy (EFT), schema therapy, and cognitive-behavioral therapy can help you identify old patterns, calm the nervous system, and create new relational habits.

Over time, the therapy relationship itself often serves as a secure base, making it easier to bring those new ways of relating into your everyday life.

Patience and predictability are key. Your partner may need more reassurance than you thought, so offering it consistently and directly can ease their anxiety. For example, sending a quick “thinking of you” text before a long meeting or confirming plans in advance can make a big difference.

At the same time, it’s important to set boundaries around what you can realistically give. A helpful approach is to offer what you can with warmth, and state what you can’t with clarity. That way, your partner feels cared for without you becoming overextended.

#9549. How Your Imagination Can Work for You or Against You

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

I have a pretty vivid imagination, sometimes for the good, sometimes not. I love it when it helps me to create new stories or songs, or when I can daydream about fun times ahead. But it can also lead to fear or worry, like when I imagine something terrible befalling the people or places I love.

Is there some way to nurture the positive aspects of imagination while minimizing the problematic? According to Cassandra Vieten, director of research at the Arthur C. Clarke Center for Human Imagination, there is. In her new book, Imagine That, she explains imagination’s importance in our everyday lives—a way to understand our past, navigate the present, and explore future possibilities. If we learn more about its inner workings, she argues, we can use it more consciously and deliberately to create the kind of life we want.

“Imagination is something we all possess, something we can all practice, for free and with equal opportunity,” says Vieten. “When someone develops this capacity, they gain something almost magical: the ability to see multiple futures simultaneously and navigate toward the preferred ones.”

Many of us tend to conflate imagination with creativity, thinking that being able to imagine new ideas is the same as bringing them to fruition. While the two may indeed be related, this is far too limited a view of what imagination can be, writes Vieten.

“Imagination is an essential, foundational capacity that allows us to simulate reality and transcend it to explore possibilities beyond the known,” she says.

In our everyday lives, imagination is what helps us make predictions as well as come up with novel (or creative) ideas. For example, we might imagine how stopping for a coffee on our way to work will help us focus (simulation imagination, based on past experience). But we might also use our imagination to transcend what’s known and come up with a totally new innovation or product idea once we arrive at the office (generative imagination).

“Imagination weaves throughout the fabric of our cognitive, sensory, and relational lives—you are constantly speculating, visualizing, rehearsing, wondering,” she writes.

These types of imagination show up differently in the brain, writes Vieten. Simulation is primarily centered in the default mode network (DMN), a part of the brain that remains active when we aren’t engaging in a specific task. The DMN is where we tend to mull over future interactions, plans, or options, often subconsciously (or even unconsciously).

Generative imagination, on the other hand, comes by freeing ourselves from the DMN’s limitations (or, some would say, tyranny). If we can get out of the everyday chatter and let our minds truly wander freely around disparate parts of the brain, making new neural connections, we have a better chance of generating something truly unique.

“Rather than simulating or iterating, comparing and contrasting, generative imagination is focused on combining, reconfiguring, or transcending existing knowledge to generate novel outputs,” writes Vieten.

Either way, imagination isn’t frivolous, she writes; it’s important for our everyday functioning as well as creative self-expression. It helps us solve problems, while also expanding possibilities of what could be, giving us “the gift of wonder, whimsy, and surprise, the whoas and the wows of our lives,” she writes.

Imagination can sometimes be problematic, though. For example, we might imagine that our spouse is mad at us and worry about what might happen when she gets home from work when, actually, she’s not mad at all. This can cause us needless worry, not to mention potentially trigger a fight.

We can also imagine that other people are unpleasant or even dangerous based on untested biases. These can be formed in part via our imagination, which tries to prepare us for unknown encounters, often behind the scenes at an unconscious level.

“We regularly imagine entire narratives, scenes, and interactions without intending to or even knowing we’re doing it,” writes Vieten.

Our imagination is often busy filling in the missing parts of our memories and perceptions, which are by nature incomplete. Memories, rather than being etched in our minds, are recreated (and often changed) each time they’re recalled. Similarly, we can’t perceive everything at once, so our imagination completes the picture for us, adding interpretations, too. This means it’s easy to corrupt memories or miss details of a situation—which can sometimes lead to problems (think eyewitness accounts of crimes, for example).

Understanding these darker sides of imagination can help us tame them somewhat, says Vieten. “You can practice bringing greater attention to what you are imagining, recognize it as imagination, and decide whether it holds useful information, is irrelevant, or is actually causing harm.”

While the book covers the neuroscience behind imagination, it’s also about how to harness our imagination more effectively. Your personal imagination style may depend, in part, on your genetics (such as neurodiversity), culture, and life experiences. Understanding this can help you figure out where you might want to try moving the needle one way or the other.

To assess your own imaginative strengths and weaknesses, here are some key imagination modes Vieten outlines in her book.

1. Receptiveness. “How willing you are to imagine—and how receptive you are to whatever bubbles up.” If you are high in receptivity, you may find it easy to do guided visualizations, for example; if low in receptivity, you may be less willing to imagine unknown scenarios.

2. Presence. How much do you embody your imagined experiences? If you tend to be absorbed, immersed, and emotionally involved in imagined scenarios, you’re high in presence; if you tend to observe these imaginings from a distance, you’re less so.

3. Embellishment. “How vivid, detailed, and elaborate people make their imaginings.” Those high in embellishment can imagine intricate scenarios with much more detail, clarity, nuance, and complexity. Those low in embellishment might be more “big picture” folks, who may not be able to conjure up details as much.

4. Originality. How much your imagination is fueled by what is or could be, based on reality, versus how much it veers from that and is based more on fantasy and novelty.

5. Temporality. How much your imagination is associated with time (in other words, assessing the past or projecting into the future) versus how much it is agnostic around time (not based on any particular time). (Vieten admits the science on this mode is not completely settled, but says there appear to be some differences in how people engage with time while imagining.)

Each of these modes has pros and cons, she argues. For example, being high in receptivity may mean you’re more cognitively flexible and open to new experiences, but can also mean you’re overly compliant and easily manipulated. Similarly, the upside of being high in originality is that it can fuel advancements in art and science, though it can lead to boredom with everyday life.

Considering my own strengths and weaknesses, I noticed that I seem to be high in receptivity and embodiment, but low in embellishment and originality (and mixed when it comes to temporality). Recognizing this makes me think about paying more attention to details in my environment and playing around with more fantastical ideas, especially if I’m wanting to fuel my creativity.

To that end, Vieten provides avenues for stretching our imagination in different ways. Some ideas for accessing different aspects of imagination deliberately include rehearsing something before doing it, brainstorming ideas, engaging all of our senses when imagining something, reframing an idea from a different perspective, and freewriting.

Vieten also suggests creating environments conducive to being more spontaneously creative. Setting time aside to daydream, being in solitude where your mind can wander, taking walks in the woods to de-stress, or, possibly, taking psychedelic drugs (in a safe, controlled environment) can all help us disengage our DMN and allow creative thoughts to enter more freely.

“One of the key ways to make imagination welcome is to remove the practical pressures of the world,” she writes.

Imagine That is full of suggestions for unleashing your imagination, all based on the emerging science of imagination that Vieten and her colleagues (and others) are exploring.

But while the book reads mostly as a self-help guide, there’s also an important message about why using our imagination is beneficial to society as a whole. Too many of us are experiencing the hopelessness and despair that come with being alive right now, writes Vieten. It’s too easy to get lost in the negative news cycles and focus on all of the problems in the world, making it more difficult to imagine anything better for our collective future.

Learning how to engage our imagination more readily can create a sense of hope in our current situation. Not only can it bring more joy and aliveness to our individual lives, countering malaise, it can also lead to new ways of collaborating with others and innovating to solve societal problems, thereby providing a better life for everyone.

“So many of the issues facing us locally and globally are rooted in our collective inability to imagine new solutions, alternative futures, creative pathways forward that could build a world that promotes thriving for all,” writes Vieten. “My deepest hope is that [you] take a deeper dive into the science, the practice, and the magic of imagination and [see] how it can re-enchant your life and our world.”

Jill Suttie, Psy.D., is Greater Good’s former book review editor and now serves as a staff writer and contributing editor for the magazine. She received her doctorate of psychology from the University of San Francisco in 1998 and was a psychologist in private practice before coming to Greater Good.

While drug-induced mystical experiences can have benefits, research suggests they may not be enough to create lasting change.

Despite how advanced robots have become, getting them to feel the way humans do is an incredibly complex challenge.
